book_skeleton.subject: chemistry

chapters.title: Chemical Reactions and Equations
chapters.summary: This chapter explores how to recognise when a chemical reaction has taken place through everyday examples and hands-on activities. It introduces the writing and balancing of chemical equations and classifies the major types of chemical reactions.

book_skeleton.subject_overview: This textbook introduces the fundamentals of chemical reactions and how they are represented through equations. It connects everyday observations to the underlying chemical changes that govern matter transformations.

events.text: Word equation = shorthand for a reaction
Reactants, then arrow, then product
Q: Write the word-equation for burning magnesium ribbon in oxygen.
Magnesium + Oxygen (reactants, left-hand side)
Magnesium + Oxygen → Magnesium oxide
Magnesium + Oxygen → Magnesium oxide
Equation: reactants (left) arrow products (right), all as formulae
Skeletal equation = formulae only, not yet checked
Atoms in equals atoms out, for every element

events.latex: \text{atoms of each element}_{\text{reactants}} = \text{atoms of each element}_{\text{products}}

events.text: Adjust front coefficients until both tallies match
Big numbers in front, never the small subscripts
Reaction = break old bonds, make new bonds
Same atoms, new arrangement
Two or more reactants join to form ONE product = combination reaction
Releases heat = exothermic
Many combination reactions are exothermic
Decomposition = one splits into many
Decomposition needs energy: heat, light, or electricity
Q: Heat solid lead nitrate. What are the products?
Products: lead oxide (s) + nitrogen dioxide (g) + oxygen (g)
Q: About 2 g of white silver chloride is placed in sunlight. What happens?
White silver chloride in sunlight turns grey (silver metal forms)
Silver chloride decomposes into silver and chlorine gas
Q: Pass electricity through acidified water and identify the gases produced.
Bubbles form at both electrodes; gases collect in the two inverted test tubes.
Volume of one gas is double the other (hydrogen = 2 x oxygen).
Water decomposes into hydrogen and oxygen; hydrogen is collected in double the volume of oxygen.
One substance to many; powered by heat, light or electricity
More reactive metal displaces less reactive metal from its compound
Lower metal can't displace higher
Q: Why does an iron nail in copper sulphate solution turn brownish while the blue colour fades?
Two nails immersed in test tube B for 20 minutes; one nail kept aside.
Result: nails become brownish, blue colour fades.
Iron displaces copper: Fe + CuSO4 → FeSO4 + Cu — a displacement reaction.
Q: Zn + CuSO4 and Pb + CuCl2 — what gets displaced?
Zn and Pb, being more reactive than Cu, displace copper from its compounds.
Reactivity series decides who displaces whom
Each compound = positive part + negative part
Double displacement = two compounds swap partners
Insoluble solid that drops out = precipitate
aq = dissolved, s = solid precipitate
Gains oxygen = oxidised
Loses oxygen = reduced
One oxidised, one reduced, together
Q: Heat about 1 g copper powder in a china dish. Why does its surface turn black?
Surface becomes coated with black copper(II) oxide
Copper is oxidised to black copper(II) oxide: 2Cu + O2 → 2CuO
Q: Hydrogen gas is passed over heated copper oxide. What happens?
Copper oxide is reduced; hydrogen is oxidised - a redox reaction
Carbon gains oxygen, so carbon is oxidised to carbon monoxide
Zinc oxide loses oxygen, so zinc oxide is reduced to zinc
Carbon is oxidised to carbon monoxide; zinc oxide is reduced to zinc
Hydrochloric acid is oxidised to chlorine
Manganese dioxide is reduced to manganese chloride
Hydrochloric acid is oxidised to chlorine; manganese dioxide is reduced to manganese chloride
Oxygen handed off: one gains, one loses
metal + moisture, air, acids
Corrosion = a metal being slowly attacked and eaten by its surroundings
Rancidity = oxidation of fats and oils by air
Air-tight containers limit oxygen contact
Antioxidants are added to react with oxygen first
Chip bags flushed with nitrogen, not air
No oxygen, no rancidity

chapters.narration_text:
<<TOPIC_START:topic:chemistry:chemical_reactions_and_equations:1_1>>
Imagine a thin strip of metal that bursts into a blinding white flame, and when the light dies, all that's left is a little heap of white powder. That strip is magnesium ribbon, and that white powder is something brand new called magnesium oxide. The magnesium grabbed oxygen out of the air and became a completely different substance. <<PAUSE:short>> <<SECTION:Describing a reaction|id=sec-1>> So how do we describe what happened? You could say a whole sentence: when magnesium ribbon is burnt in oxygen, it gets converted to magnesium oxide. That's correct, but imagine writing a paragraph like that every single time you wanted to talk about a reaction. Wouldn't you want a shorter way? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> Chemists did exactly that. They invented a shorthand, and the simplest version is called a word equation. <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:chemistry:chemical_reactions_and_equations:1_1:word_equation_flow>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Word equation = shorthand for a reaction|id=text-1>> Here's the idea. The stuff you start with goes on the left. We <<FOCUS:reactant-magnesium>> start with magnesium, and we <<FOCUS:reactant-oxygen>> start with oxygen. Because there are two starting substances, we <<FOCUS:plus-sign>> join them with a plus sign, just like adding ingredients in a recipe. <<UNFOCUS>> These starting substances have a special name. <<FOCUS:reactants-bracket+reactants-label>> We call them the reactants, the things that react. <<UNFOCUS>> Now, the magnesium and oxygen turn into something new. We show 'turns into' <<FOCUS:reaction-arrow>> with an arrow, and the arrowhead points the way the reaction goes. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Reactants, then arrow, then product|id=key-1>> And where the arrow points, on the right-hand side, we write the new substance that's made: <<FOCUS:product-magnesium-oxide>> magnesium oxide. <<FOCUS:product-bracket+product-label>> That's the product. <<UNFOCUS>> Here's an example from the chapter. When we burn a magnesium ribbon in oxygen, it produces magnesium oxide. The substances that take part, <<FOCUS:reactant-magnesium+reactant-oxygen>> magnesium and oxygen, are the reactants, and the new substance formed, <<FOCUS:product-magnesium-oxide>> magnesium oxide, is the product. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Write the word-equation for burning magnesium ribbon in oxygen.|id=ex-q-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> We start by placing the reactants on the left-hand side. Magnesium and oxygen are what we begin with, so we write magnesium plus oxygen on the left. <<WRITE_STEP:Magnesium + Oxygen (reactants, left-hand side)|id=ex-step-1-1>> Next we <<TRACE:reaction-arrow>> draw an arrow pointing toward the product, and on the right-hand side we write the product, magnesium oxide. The arrow shows the direction of the reaction, <<FOCUS:reactants-bracket+product-bracket>> from reactants to product. <<WRITE_STEP:Magnesium + Oxygen → Magnesium oxide|id=ex-step-1-2>> <<UNFOCUS>> And so the complete word-equation is: magnesium plus oxygen gives magnesium oxide. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Magnesium + Oxygen → Magnesium oxide|id=ex-ans-1>> Look at the whole thing now: magnesium plus oxygen, arrow, magnesium oxide. Reactants on the left, the new product on the right. <<PAUSE:short>> So remember this shape: <<FOCUS:reactants-bracket>> reactants on the left, <<FOCUS:reaction-arrow>> an arrow that means 'turns into' pointing right, and the <<FOCUS:product-bracket>> products on the right. <<UNFOCUS>> That single line tells the whole story of the reaction. <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:chemistry:chemical_reactions_and_equations:1_1_1>>
Strike a ribbon of magnesium and it flares with a blinding white light — but how do you write down what just happened without scribbling a whole sentence? <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:chemistry:chemical_reactions_and_equations:1_1_1:word_to_symbol_equation>> In words you'd say: magnesium reacts with oxygen to give magnesium oxide. True, but long and clumsy — and imagine writing that for every reaction. <<SECTION:Writing a Chemical Equation|id=sec-1>> So chemists found a shorter, smarter way: instead of spelling out names, they swap in each substance's chemical formula. <<PAUSE:short>> Magnesium is simply Mg. Oxygen in the air travels as a pair of atoms locked together, so we write it as O two. And magnesium oxide is M g O. Now here's the real question: where do these formulae go, and what holds the whole thing together? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> The substances you start with — magnesium and oxygen — go on the left. We call them the reactants. Then we draw an arrow pointing right. Read that arrow as the words 'turns into' — it shows the direction the reaction goes. <<PAUSE:short>> And on the right side goes what you end up with: magnesium oxide, the product. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Equation: reactants (left) arrow products (right), all as formulae|id=key-1>> Put it together and the whole reaction collapses into one tidy line: Mg plus O two, arrow, M g O. <<PAUSE:short>> Magnesium plus oxygen, arrow meaning turns into, gives magnesium oxide. <<WRITE_EQUATION:Mg + O_2 \rightarrow MgO|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Skeletal equation = formulae only, not yet checked|id=text-1>> This compact form, written straight from the formulae, is called a skeletal chemical equation — the bare bones of the reaction. One quiet thing to notice: oxygen had to be written as O two, not just O, because that's how it actually exists in the air — as pairs of atoms. <<PAUSE:short>> So a long sentence became a single symbolic line: formulae for the substances, an arrow for 'turns into', reactants on the left and products on the right. That's a chemical equation.

<<TOPIC_START:topic:chemistry:chemical_reactions_and_equations:1_1_2>>
<<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:chemistry:chemical_reactions_and_equations:1_1_2:atom_count_balance>> If you weigh a sealed jar before and after a reaction fizzes away inside it, the scale does not move even a hair. So where does the new stuff come from? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> The answer is that nothing new is ever made. The atoms you start with are the exact same atoms you finish with, just rearranged into new partners. <<PAUSE:short>> <<SECTION:Conservation of mass|id=sec-1>> This is the law of conservation of mass you met last year. Mass can neither be created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction. <<WRITE_KEY:Atoms in equals atoms out, for every element|id=key-1>> Said in plain terms, the number of atoms of each element stays exactly the same before and after. <<FOCUS:reactant-side>> Count them on the left, <<FOCUS:product-side>> count them on the right, and the two counts must match. <<PAUSE:short>> For every element, the number of atoms on <<FOCUS:reactant-tally+product-tally>> the reactant side equals the number of atoms on the product side. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\text{atoms of each element}_{\text{reactants}} = \text{atoms of each element}_{\text{products}}|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<UNFOCUS>> Watch how we check this. <<FOCUS:reactant-tally>> On the reactant side I tally up each kind of atom one element at a time. <<FOCUS:product-tally>> Now the product side. <<UNFOCUS>> If every element's tally on the right matches the left, the equation is already balanced. Here is a reaction where zinc meets sulphuric acid to give zinc sulphate and hydrogen, and the count already matches on both sides. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\mathrm{Zn} + \mathrm{H_2SO_4} \rightarrow \mathrm{ZnSO_4} + \mathrm{H_2}|id=eq-2|boxed>> But what happens when a count does not match? Say there are four oxygen atoms on one side but only one on the other. Can we just shrink the formula? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> No. The little <<FOCUS:subscript-lock>> subscript numbers inside a formula are locked. <<UNFOCUS>> Changing water from H two O to H O would turn it into a completely different substance. <<PAUSE:short>> Instead, we place <<FOCUS:coefficient-slot>> a big number in front of the whole formula. That number <<FOCUS:coeff-ring>> multiplies every atom in the cluster at once, like buying two identical boxes instead of repacking one. <<WRITE_STEP:Adjust front coefficients until both tallies match|id=step-1>> We keep adjusting those front numbers until the <<FOCUS:reactant-tally+product-tally>> reactant tally and the product tally agree for every single element. <<WRITE_TEXT:Big numbers in front, never the small subscripts|id=text-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> So the whole method is just bookkeeping for atoms. <<FOCUS:coefficient-slot>> Change the big numbers in front, <<FOCUS:subscript-lock>> never the small subscripts inside. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> And when both tallies finally match, every atom is accounted for, the mass is conserved, and the scale on that sealed jar stays perfectly still. <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:chemistry:chemical_reactions_and_equations:1_2>>
Burn a log down to a pile of ash, weigh it, and the ash is lighter than the log you started with. Yet chemistry insists not one atom was destroyed. So where did the missing mass go? Hold that question, because the answer rewrites what you think a reaction even is. <<PAUSE:long>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:chemistry:chemical_reactions_and_equations:1_2:bond_rearrangement>> <<SECTION:Atoms are stubborn|id=sec-1>> Here is the first stubborn rule. During an ordinary chemical reaction, <<FOCUS:reactant-cluster>> an atom of oxygen stays an atom of oxygen. <<UNFOCUS>> It never becomes carbon, never becomes anything else. <<PAUSE:short>> And atoms never vanish into nothing, and they never appear from nowhere. Whatever you started with, you still have, every last one. <<PAUSE:short>> But if the atoms are all the same and all still here, then how on earth do we get a brand-new substance out the other side? <<PAUSE:long>> Watch the <<FOCUS:old-bond>> lines holding these atoms together. Those lines are bonds, and as the reaction begins, the old bonds break apart. <<PAUSE:short>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Reaction = break old bonds, make new bonds|id=key-1>> Now the very same atoms link up in a new pattern, and <<FOCUS:new-bond>> fresh bonds form. <<UNFOCUS>> The atoms are old; the arrangement is new. <<PAUSE:short>> And <<FOCUS:product-cluster>> there is your new substance. <<UNFOCUS>> Same building blocks, a different structure. That is the whole secret of a chemical reaction. <<WRITE_TEXT:Same atoms, new arrangement|id=text-1>> Count them. Every kind of atom appears exactly <<FOCUS:atom-count-tally>> as many times on the right as it did on the left. <<UNFOCUS>> Nothing gained, nothing lost. <<PAUSE:short>> So back to our log. The missing mass did not disappear; its atoms floated off invisibly as carbon dioxide and water vapour. Catch those gases and the weight is exactly the same. Remember this and reactions stop being magic: atoms are never made, destroyed, or transformed, they are only rearranged, by breaking old bonds and making new ones. <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:chemistry:chemical_reactions_and_equations:1_2_1>>
<<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:chemistry:chemical_reactions_and_equations:1_2_1:combination_flow>> Drop a little white powder into water, touch the beaker, and your fingers feel heat — no flame, yet the glass is warm. Something just happened inside. That white powder is <<FOCUS:reactant-cao>> calcium oxide, which people call quick lime. <<SECTION:Combination Reaction|id=sec-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> On the left of our story we have two separate things. <<FOCUS:reactant-cao>> Calcium oxide here, and <<FOCUS:reactant-water>> plain water here. <<FOCUS:reactant-cao+reactant-water>> Two reactants, sitting apart, waiting to meet. <<UNFOCUS>> Now watch what happens when they meet. They join together and <<FOCUS:product-caoh2>> become a single new substance. <<WRITE_KEY:Two or more reactants join to form ONE product = combination reaction|id=key-1>> This is the whole idea: <<FOCUS:reactant-cao+reactant-water>> two or more things go in, and exactly <<FOCUS:product-caoh2>> one new product comes out. That is a <<FOCUS:arrow-combine>> combination reaction. <<PAUSE:short>> The one product here is <<FOCUS:product-caoh2>> calcium hydroxide, the substance we call slaked lime. <<UNFOCUS>> Two became one. <<PAUSE:short>> But here is the puzzle: why did the beaker get warm? Nothing was burning, so where did the heat come from? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> When the two reactants lock together into the new product, the rearranging of their atoms <<FOCUS:heat-glyph>> releases stored energy — and that energy escapes as heat. <<WRITE_TEXT:Releases heat = exothermic|id=text-1>> A reaction that gives out heat like this is called exothermic. <<UNFOCUS>> The warm beaker is the proof you can feel. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:reactant-cao+reactant-water>> Calcium oxide plus water combines to give a <<FOCUS:product-caoh2>> single product, calcium hydroxide, and <<FOCUS:heat-glyph>> releases heat. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\text{CaO}(s) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightarrow \text{Ca(OH)}_2(aq) + \text{Heat}|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<UNFOCUS>> So in plain words, calcium oxide plus water gives calcium hydroxide and releases heat. <<WRITE_KEY:Many combination reactions are exothermic|id=key-2>> And this heat is no accident — a great many combination reactions are exothermic, giving out warmth as the new product forms. <<PAUSE:short>> So remember the signature: <<FOCUS:arrow-combine>> count the arrows. If two or more reactants <<FOCUS:product-caoh2>> funnel into a single product, you are looking at a combination reaction — and often, you can feel it happen. <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:chemistry:chemical_reactions_and_equations:1_2_2>>
<<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:chemistry:chemical_reactions_and_equations:1_2_2:decomposition_split>> What if I told you that one single thing, sitting quietly in a dish, can split itself into two completely different things — just because the sun shone on it? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> That white powder is silver chloride, and after a while in sunlight it turns grey. The grey is silver metal, and a greenish gas, chlorine, has quietly slipped away into the air. <<SECTION:Decomposition|id=sec-1>> So one substance became two simpler ones. That is the whole idea of a decomposition reaction: <<FOCUS:parent-compound>> a single substance breaks down into <<FOCUS:product-one+product-two>> two or more simpler substances. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Decomposition = one splits into many|id=text-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> Watch the picture. <<FOCUS:parent-compound>> One block on the left, but on the right it has <<FOCUS:product-one+product-two>> split into two separate blocks. And here is <<FOCUS:product-two>> the second piece. <<FOCUS:parent-compound>> One parent has <<FOCUS:product-one+product-two>> become two children, each simpler than what we started with. <<UNFOCUS>> This is exactly the opposite of a combination reaction, where many things join into one. Here we take one thing and pull it apart. But splitting something apart is hard work. So here is the catch: where does the push to break it come from? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Decomposition needs energy: heat, light, or electricity|id=key-1>> It comes <<FOCUS:energy-arrow+energy-label>> from energy we supply. Every decomposition <<FOCUS:energy-squiggle>> needs energy fed in — and it arrives as heat, as light, or as electricity. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> When the energy is heat, we give it a special name: thermal decomposition. Heat lead nitrate, and one solid crumbles into a solid plus two different gases. With our silver chloride, the energy was light instead. Sunlight alone was enough to tear it into silver and chlorine. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:parent-compound>> Two units of silver chloride, when sunlight is supplied, <<FOCUS:product-one+product-two>> break down into two units of silver metal plus one molecule of chlorine gas. <<WRITE_EQUATION:2AgCl(s) \xrightarrow{\text{sunlight}} 2Ag(s) + Cl_2(g)|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<UNFOCUS>> Here's an example from the chapter. We take solid lead nitrate and heat it strongly. The heat is the energy source that drives this reaction, and our job is to figure out what lead nitrate breaks down into. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Heat solid lead nitrate. What are the products?|id=ex-q-1>> We start by writing the reactant. Solid lead nitrate, written as two P b N O three twice, <<FOCUS:energy-arrow+energy-label>> with heat supplied above the arrow. <<UNFOCUS>> Because a single compound is being split apart by heat, this is a thermal decomposition. <<WRITE_STEP:2Pb(NO3)2 (s) --Heat-->|id=ex-step-1-1>> On heating, the lead nitrate breaks into three products: solid lead oxide, nitrogen dioxide gas, and oxygen gas. <<WRITE_EQUATION:2Pb(NO_3)_2(s) \xrightarrow{\text{Heat}} 2PbO(s) + 4NO_2(g) + O_2(g)|id=ex-eq-1>> So the balanced reaction gives two P b O solid, four N O two gas, and one O two gas. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Products: lead oxide (s) + nitrogen dioxide (g) + oxygen (g)|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. We take about two grams of silver chloride, which starts out white, in a china dish, and we place this dish in sunlight for some time. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: About 2 g of white silver chloride is placed in sunlight. What happens?|id=ex-q-1>> We observe the dish carefully. After being placed in sunlight, the white silver chloride slowly turns grey, and this grey colour is due to the formation of silver metal. <<WRITE_STEP:White silver chloride in sunlight turns grey (silver metal forms)|id=ex-step-1-1>> So light supplies the energy that decomposes the silver chloride, and the products are silver and chlorine gas. The reaction is two A g C l solid, under sunlight, gives two A g solid plus C l two gas. <<WRITE_EQUATION:2AgCl(s) \xrightarrow{Sunlight} 2Ag(s) + Cl_2(g)|id=ex-eq-1>> <<WRITE_ANSWER:Silver chloride decomposes into silver and chlorine gas|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter — the electrolysis of water. We take a plastic mug fitted with two carbon electrodes, and we connect these electrodes to a six volt battery. The mug is filled with water, plus a few drops of dilute sulphuric acid to help conduct the current. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Pass electricity through acidified water and identify the gases produced.|id=ex-q-1>> Now we set up the collection. We take two test tubes filled with water and invert them over the two carbon electrodes. When we switch on the current, we observe the formation of bubbles at both the electrodes, and these bubbles displace the water in the test tubes. <<WRITE_STEP:Bubbles form at both electrodes; gases collect in the two inverted test tubes.|id=ex-step-1-1>> <<PAUSE:short>> Notice carefully: one gas is collected in double the volume of the other — the hydrogen is collected in twice the amount of the oxygen. <<WRITE_STEP:Volume of one gas is double the other (hydrogen = 2 x oxygen).|id=ex-step-1-2>> Finally, we test these gases one by one by bringing a burning candle close to the mouth of the test tubes. The larger volume of gas, the hydrogen, burns with a pop, while the oxygen relights the flame. So acidified water decomposes into hydrogen and oxygen, with hydrogen collected in double the volume of oxygen. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Water decomposes into hydrogen and oxygen; hydrogen is collected in double the volume of oxygen.|id=ex-ans-1>> And if you pass electricity through water, it splits too — into hydrogen and oxygen gas, bubbling off at the two electrodes. <<WRITE_KEY:One substance to many; powered by heat, light or electricity|id=key-2>> So remember the shape of it: one substance breaking down into two or more simpler ones, every time powered by heat, light, or electricity. <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:chemistry:chemical_reactions_and_equations:1_2_3>>
Drop a shiny iron nail into clear blue copper sulphate solution, wait twenty minutes, and you pull out a nail coated in reddish-brown copper while the blue slowly fades to pale green. <<SECTION:Displacement Reactions|id=sec-1>> Two things changed at once, and that is the whole story: the nail gained a reddish-brown layer, and the blue colour drained away. So here is the honest question: where did that reddish-brown coating come from, and where did the blue colour go? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> The blue colour comes from copper sitting inside the solution, and the reddish-brown coat is that very same copper, now stuck onto the nail. The copper left the solution and landed on the iron. <<WRITE_KEY:More reactive metal displaces less reactive metal from its compound|id=key-1>> And this is the heart of it: a more reactive metal pushes a less reactive metal out of its compound and takes its place. The iron is more reactive, so it shoves the copper out. <<PAUSE:short>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:chemistry:chemical_reactions_and_equations:1_2_3:reactivity_ladder>> To see why iron wins and copper does not, <<FOCUS:reactivity-arrow+reactivity-label>> picture the metals on a ladder, ranked by how reactive they are. <<FOCUS:iron-rung>> Iron sits up here, higher on the ladder, <<FOCUS:copper-rung>> while copper sits lower down. <<UNFOCUS>> Higher means more eager to react. Because iron is above copper, <<TRACE:displacement-direction>> iron can reach down and displace copper from its compound. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Lower metal can't displace higher|id=text-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> But run it the other way: would a copper nail dropped into iron sulphate ever pull the iron out? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> No, nothing happens, because <<FOCUS:copper-rung+iron-rung>> copper is below iron on the ladder. The reactivity series decides the winner, and <<FOCUS:reactivity-arrow>> a lower metal can never displace a higher one. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> Here's an example from the chapter. We take three iron nails and clean them by rubbing with sandpaper. Then we take two test tubes, marked A and B, and in each we pour about ten milliliters of copper sulphate solution, which is a clear blue color. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Why does an iron nail in copper sulphate solution turn brownish while the blue colour fades?|id=ex-q-1>> Iron metal reacts with copper sulphate solution to give iron sulphate solution and solid copper. <<WRITE_EQUATION:Fe(s) + CuSO_4(aq) \rightarrow FeSO_4(aq) + Cu(s)|id=eq-1|boxed>> Now we tie two iron nails together with a thread and immerse them carefully in test tube B for about twenty minutes, while we keep one nail aside for comparison. After twenty minutes, when we take the nails out, the nails turn brownish and the blue color of the solution fades. <<WRITE_STEP:Two nails immersed in test tube B for 20 minutes; one nail kept aside.|id=ex-step-1>> <<WRITE_STEP:Result: nails become brownish, blue colour fades.|id=ex-step-2>> This happens because iron is more reactive than copper, so iron displaces copper from the copper sulphate solution. The reaction is iron plus copper sulphate gives iron sulphate plus copper. The brown coating is the copper deposited on the nail, and the blue fades because the copper sulphate is used up. So the answer is that a displacement reaction takes place. <<WRITE_EQUATION:Fe(s) + CuSO_4(aq) \rightarrow FeSO_4(aq) + Cu(s)|id=ex-eq-1>> <<WRITE_ANSWER:Iron displaces copper: Fe + CuSO4 → FeSO4 + Cu — a displacement reaction.|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. We look at two more displacement reactions. In the first, zinc reacts with copper sulphate. In the second, lead reacts with copper chloride. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Zn + CuSO4 and Pb + CuCl2 — what gets displaced?|id=ex-q-1>> Let's work them out. Zinc plus copper sulphate gives zinc sulphate plus copper. <<WRITE_STEP:Zn(s) + CuSO4(aq) -> ZnSO4(aq) + Cu(s)|id=ex-step-1-1>> And lead plus copper chloride gives lead chloride plus copper. <<WRITE_STEP:Pb(s) + CuCl2(aq) -> PbCl2(aq) + Cu(s)|id=ex-step-1-2>> Why does this happen? Because zinc and lead are more reactive than copper, so each of them pushes copper out of its compound. The answer is that copper is displaced in both reactions. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Zn and Pb, being more reactive than Cu, displace copper from its compounds.|id=ex-ans-1>> Now we can write what actually happened in symbols: iron plus copper sulphate gives iron sulphate plus copper. <<WRITE_KEY:Reactivity series decides who displaces whom|id=key-2>> So remember the whole idea in one line: the higher metal in the reactivity series displaces the lower one out of its compound, and never the reverse. <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:chemistry:chemical_reactions_and_equations:1_2_4>>
Two perfectly clear liquids. You pour one into the other, and suddenly the mixture turns milky white with a solid settling at the bottom. Nobody added a powder, so where did that solid come from? <<PAUSE:long>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:chemistry:chemical_reactions_and_equations:1_2_4:partner_swap>> <<SECTION:Double Displacement|id=sec-1>> The answer is hiding inside the word displacement, which simply means swapping, and double, which means it happens twice. Think of it like a dance. Each clear liquid holds a compound made of two parts: a positive partner and a negative partner, drifting around dissolved in the water. <<WRITE_TEXT:Each compound = positive part + negative part|id=text-1>> In our case one liquid carries <<FOCUS:sodium-ion+sulphate-ion>> sodium holding hands with sulphate, and the other carries <<FOCUS:barium-ion+chloride-ion>> barium holding hands with chloride. <<UNFOCUS>> Now mix them, and the music starts. <<FOCUS:swap-arrows>> The partners swap: the positive part of one compound goes looking for the negative part of the other. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Double displacement = two compounds swap partners|id=key-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> That is the whole idea: two dissolved compounds trade partners, positive of one joining negative of the other. That is double displacement. <<PAUSE:short>> But here is the twist. <<FOCUS:barium-ion+sulphate-ion>> When barium meets sulphate, the new pair they make refuses to stay dissolved in water. <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> So that brand new barium sulphate pair <<FOCUS:precipitate-solid>> clumps together and sinks. <<UNFOCUS>> That cloudy white solid you saw was created right there in the swap, born from two clear liquids. Meanwhile <<FOCUS:dissolved-product>> sodium and chloride happily pair up too, but they stay spread out and dissolved, invisible in the clear part of the liquid. <<UNFOCUS>> Sodium sulphate plus barium chloride gives barium sulphate, the solid, plus sodium chloride, which stays dissolved. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4(aq) + \text{BaCl}_2(aq) \rightarrow \text{BaSO}_4(s) + 2\text{NaCl}(aq)|id=eq-1|boxed>> An insoluble solid that drops out of a solution like this has a special name: <<FOCUS:precipitate-solid>> a precipitate. <<UNFOCUS>> And any reaction that makes one is called a precipitation reaction. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Insoluble solid that drops out = precipitate|id=key-2>> So whenever a partner swap produces something insoluble, watch for the cloudiness, that solid is your precipitate forming before your eyes. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:aq = dissolved, s = solid precipitate|id=text-2>> Notice the labels: the things that <<FOCUS:dissolved-label>> stay dissolved are marked watery, and <<FOCUS:precipitate-label>> the solid that drops out is marked solid. <<UNFOCUS>> That single label tells you which partner pair became the precipitate. <<PAUSE:short>>

Copper was oxidised to copper oxide. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:copper-block>> Two units of copper combine with <<FOCUS:oxygen-molecule>> one molecule of oxygen gas to give <<FOCUS:copper-oxide-block>> two units of black copper oxide. <<WRITE_EQUATION:2Cu + O_2 \xrightarrow{\text{Heat}} 2CuO|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<UNFOCUS>> So here is a fair question. The <<FOCUS:copper-oxide-block>> copper oxide lost oxygen, but the <<FOCUS:hydrogen-molecule>> hydrogen gained it. <<WRITE_KEY:One oxidised, one reduced, together|id=key-3>> <<UNFOCUS>> So in one single reaction, one reactant is reduced while the other is oxidised, at the very same time. They always come as a pair. <<PAUSE:short>> Here's an example from the chapter. We take about one gram of copper powder and heat it in a china dish. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Heat about 1 g copper powder in a china dish. Why does its surface turn black?|id=ex-q-1>> As the copper powder is heated, its surface becomes coated with a black substance. That black coating is copper two oxide, because oxygen from the air is added to the copper. <<WRITE_STEP:Surface becomes coated with black copper(II) oxide|id=ex-step-1-1>> So the reaction is this: two copper plus one oxygen gas, on heating, gives two copper oxide. <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:chemistry:chemical_reactions_and_equations:1_3_1:corrosion_three_metals>> Leave a shiny new iron nail outside for a few weeks, and it comes back covered in a flaky, reddish-brown powder. The shine is gone, and <<FOCUS:iron-nail-rusted>> in its place is rust. <<UNFOCUS>> We call this the rusting of iron. But here's a question worth pausing on: is iron the only metal this happens to, or is something bigger going on? <<PAUSE:long>> <<FOCUS:copper-shiny>> Look at copper. A bright orange statue left outside slowly grows a <<FOCUS:copper-green>> dull green coating. <<UNFOCUS>> You've seen this on old domes and rooftops. <<FOCUS:silver-shiny>> And silver. A gleaming spoon left in a drawer <<FOCUS:silver-black>> slowly turns black. <<UNFOCUS>> That's not dirt you can wipe off, it's the silver itself changing. <<PAUSE:short>> So no, iron isn't special. <<FOCUS:iron-nail-rusted>> Rust, <<FOCUS:copper-green>> green copper, and <<FOCUS:silver-black>> black silver are all the same story: a metal being attacked by the stuff around it. <<PAUSE:short>> <<SECTION:What corrosion is|id=sec-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> What's doing the attacking? Mostly <<FOCUS:attack-arrows+attack-label>> moisture and the air, sometimes acids. <<WRITE_TEXT:metal + moisture, air, acids|id=text-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> When a metal is slowly eaten away like this, we say it corrodes. <<WRITE_KEY:Corrosion = a metal being slowly attacked and eaten by its surroundings|id=key-1>> That process has a name: corrosion. Corrosion is a metal being slowly attacked and eaten away by the substances around it. <<PAUSE:short>> And remember oxidation from last time? Corrosion is exactly that, happening to a metal: the metal loses electrons to oxygen and is oxidised, which is why the surface changes colour. <<PAUSE:short>> This isn't just a curiosity. Corrosion eats car bodies, bridges, ships, and railings, and rusting iron especially costs an enormous amount of money to replace every single year. <<PAUSE:short>> So when you next spot rust on a gate, green on a statue, or black on a spoon, you're seeing one idea in three costumes: a metal quietly being attacked by the world around it. <<PAUSE:short>>

Open a packet of chips that's been sitting in the cupboard for months, and it hits you — that stale, almost paint-like smell. What actually happened to those chips? The chips didn't rot the way fruit goes mouldy. Something quieter happened — the oxygen in the air slowly attacked the oil they were fried in. <<SECTION:Rancidity|id=sec-1>> Fats and oils react with oxygen from the air in a chemical reaction. And you already know its name — this is oxidation, the same kind of reaction where a substance gains oxygen. <<WRITE_KEY:Rancidity = oxidation of fats and oils by air|id=key-1>> When fats and oils are oxidised, we say they go rancid — their smell and taste change for the worse. That single word, rancidity, is the whole story. <<PAUSE:short>> Here's the honest question, though: if it's just oxygen doing this, why doesn't every packet of chips on the shelf taste terrible the day you buy it? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> Because oxidation is slow, and manufacturers fight it. The trick is simple — if oxygen causes rancidity, then take the oxygen away. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_STEP:Air-tight containers limit oxygen contact|id=step-1>> That's why oily food is sealed in air-tight containers — less air touching the fat means slower oxidation. <<WRITE_STEP:Antioxidants are added to react with oxygen first|id=step-2>> It's also why packets list antioxidants. These are substances that get oxidised instead of the fat, taking the hit so the oil stays fresh. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_STEP:Chip bags flushed with nitrogen, not air|id=step-3>> And the cleverest trick — chip manufacturers flush the bag with nitrogen gas. Nitrogen is unreactive, so with no oxygen inside, the chips simply can't go rancid. <<PAUSE:short>> Squeeze a sealed chip packet and feel how puffy it is. That cushion isn't air — it's nitrogen, quietly protecting your snack. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:No oxygen, no rancidity|id=key-2>> So next time food smells off, you'll know the culprit: oxygen oxidising the fats and oils. Keep the oxygen out, and you keep the food fresh. <<PAUSE:short>>

lecture_plan.chapter_arc: We begin by learning to recognise when a chemical change has truly happened, then build a precise language — chemical equations — to describe it, insisting that atoms are conserved so every equation must balance. From there we organise the messy variety of reactions into a handful of clear types, and finally watch those same reactions show up in the real world as rusting and spoiled food.
lecture_plan.opening_hook: A thin strip of magnesium flares into a blinding white light and leaves behind a soft white powder — something brand new that wasn't there before. How do chemists capture, write down, and even predict changes like this one?

coverage_checklist.description: Identify the observable signs that a chemical reaction has occurred (colour change, gas, heat/light, precipitate, smell) using everyday examples
Translate a word description of a reaction into a symbolic chemical equation using formulae, reactants, and products
Connect balancing equations to the law of conservation of mass and demonstrate the step-by-step balancing of a real equation
Classify reactions into combination, decomposition, displacement, and double displacement with a distinguishing example for each
Show that decomposition is the reverse of combination and that it requires an energy input (heat, light, or electricity)
Explain oxidation and reduction in terms of gain and loss of oxygen, and that they occur together
Link rusting (corrosion) and rancidity to oxidation reactions happening in everyday life, plus simple methods to prevent them

lecture_plan.closing_summary: Look back at that burning magnesium ribbon we started with: you can now recognise it as a real chemical reaction, write it as a symbolic equation, balance it so no atom is lost or created, and even name it as a combination — and an oxidation — reaction. Along the way you've learned to sort the whole zoo of chemical changes into combination, decomposition, displacement, and double displacement, and you've seen those same processes quietly at work in the rust on an old gate and the off smell of stale food. That's the power of this chapter: a single language and a handful of categories that let you describe, predict, and even control the chemistry happening all around you.

segments.narration_chapter: Imagine a thin strip of metal that bursts into a blinding white flame, and when the light dies, all that's left is a little heap of white powder. That strip is magnesium ribbon, and that white powder is something brand new called magnesium oxide. The magnesium grabbed oxygen out of the air and became a completely different substance. <<PAUSE:short>> <<SECTION:Describing a reaction|id=sec-1>> So how do we describe what happened? You could say a whole sentence: when magnesium ribbon is burnt in oxygen, it gets converted to magnesium oxide. That's correct, but imagine writing a paragraph like that every single time you wanted to talk about a reaction. Wouldn't you want a shorter way? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> Chemists did exactly that. They invented a shorthand, and the simplest version is called a word equation. <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:chemistry:chemical_reactions_and_equations:1_1:word_equation_flow>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Word equation = shorthand for a reaction|id=text-1>> Here's the idea. The stuff you start with goes on the left. We <<FOCUS:reactant-magnesium>> start with magnesium, and we <<FOCUS:reactant-oxygen>> start with oxygen. Because there are two starting substances, we <<FOCUS:plus-sign>> join them with a plus sign, just like adding ingredients in a recipe. <<UNFOCUS>> These starting substances have a special name. <<FOCUS:reactants-bracket+reactants-label>> We call them the reactants, the things that react. <<UNFOCUS>> Now, the magnesium and oxygen turn into something new. When we burn a magnesium ribbon in oxygen, it produces magnesium oxide. segments.narration_chapter: Strike a ribbon of magnesium and it flares with a blinding white light — but how do you write down what just happened without scribbling a whole sentence? <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:chemistry:chemical_reactions_and_equations:1_1_1:word_to_symbol_equation>> In words you'd say: magnesium reacts with oxygen to give magnesium oxide. True, but long and clumsy — and imagine writing that for every reaction. <<SECTION:Writing a Chemical Equation|id=sec-1>> So chemists found a shorter, smarter way: instead of spelling out names, they swap in each substance's chemical formula. <<PAUSE:short>> Magnesium is simply Mg. Oxygen in the air travels as a pair of atoms locked together, so we write it as O two. And magnesium oxide is M g O. Now here's the real question: where do these formulae go, and what holds the whole thing together? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> The substances you start with — magnesium and oxygen — go on the left. We call them the reactants. Then we draw an arrow pointing right. Read that arrow as the words 'turns into' — it shows the direction the reaction goes. <<PAUSE:short>> And on the right side goes what you end up with: magnesium oxide, the product. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Equation: reactants (left) arrow products (right), all as formulae|id=key-1>> Put it together and the whole reaction collapses into one tidy line: Mg plus O two, arrow, M g O. <<PAUSE:short>> Magnesium plus oxygen, arrow meaning turns into, gives magnesium oxide. <<WRITE_EQUATION:Mg + O_2 \rightarrow MgO|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Skeletal equation = formulae only, not yet checked|id=text-1>> This compact form, written straight from the formulae, is called a skeletal chemical equation — the bare bones of the reaction. One quiet thing to notice: oxygen had to be written as O two, not just O, because that's how it actually exists in the air — as pairs of atoms. <<PAUSE:short>> So a long sentence became a single symbolic line: formulae for the substances, an arrow for 'turns into', reactants on the left and products on the right. That's a chemical equation.

segments.narration_chapter: <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:chemistry:chemical_reactions_and_equations:1_1_2:atom_count_balance>> If you weigh a sealed jar before and after a reaction fizzes away inside it, the scale does not move even a hair. So where does the new stuff come from? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> The answer is that nothing new is ever made. The atoms you start with are the exact same atoms you finish with, just rearranged into new partners. <<PAUSE:short>> <<SECTION:Conservation of mass|id=sec-1>> This is the law of conservation of mass you met last year. Mass can neither be created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction. <<WRITE_KEY:Atoms in equals atoms out, for every element|id=key-1>> Said in plain terms, the number of atoms of each element stays exactly the same before and after. <<FOCUS:reactant-side>> Count them on the left, <<FOCUS:product-side>> count them on the right, and the two counts must match. <<PAUSE:short>> For every element, the number of atoms on <<FOCUS:reactant-tally+product-tally>> the reactant side equals the number of atoms on the product side. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\text{atoms of each element}_{\text{reactants}} = \text{atoms of each element}_{\text{products}}|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<UNFOCUS>> Watch how we check this. <<FOCUS:reactant-tally>> On the reactant side I tally up each kind of atom one element at a time. <<FOCUS:product-tally>> Now the product side. <<UNFOCUS>> If every element's tally on the right matches the left, the equation is already balanced. Here is a reaction where zinc meets sulphuric acid to give zinc sulphate and hydrogen, and the count already matches on both sides. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\mathrm{Zn} + \mathrm{H_2SO_4} \rightarrow \mathrm{ZnSO_4} + \mathrm{H_2}|id=eq-2|boxed>> But what happens when a count does not match? Can we just shrink the formula? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> No. The little <<FOCUS:subscript-lock>> subscript numbers inside a formula are locked. <<UNFOCUS>> Changing water from H two O to H O would turn it into a completely different substance. <<PAUSE:short>> Instead, we place <<FOCUS:coefficient-slot>> a big number in front of the whole formula. segments.narration_chapter: Burn a log down to a pile of ash, weigh it, and the ash is lighter than the log you started with. Yet chemistry insists not one atom was destroyed. So where did the missing mass go? Hold that question, because the answer rewrites what you think a reaction even is. <<PAUSE:long>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:chemistry:chemical_reactions_and_equations:1_2:bond_rearrangement>> <<SECTION:Atoms are stubborn|id=sec-1>> Here is the first stubborn rule. During an ordinary chemical reaction, <<FOCUS:reactant-cluster>> an atom of oxygen stays an atom of oxygen. <<UNFOCUS>> It never becomes carbon, never becomes anything else. <<PAUSE:short>> And atoms never vanish into nothing, and they never appear from nowhere. Whatever you started with, you still have, every last one. <<PAUSE:short>> But if the atoms are all the same and all still here, then how on earth do we get a brand-new substance out the other side? <<PAUSE:long>> Watch the <<FOCUS:old-bond>> lines holding these atoms together. Those lines are bonds, and as the reaction begins, the old bonds break apart. <<PAUSE:short>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Reaction = break old bonds, make new bonds|id=key-1>> Now the very same atoms link up in a new pattern, and <<FOCUS:new-bond>> fresh bonds form. <<UNFOCUS>> The atoms are old; the arrangement is new. <<PAUSE:short>> And <<FOCUS:product-cluster>> there is your new substance. <<UNFOCUS>> Same building blocks, a different structure. That is the whole secret of a chemical reaction. <<WRITE_TEXT:Same atoms, new arrangement|id=text-1>> Count them. Every kind of atom appears exactly <<FOCUS:atom-count-tally>> as many times on the right as it did on the left. <<UNFOCUS>> Nothing gained, nothing lost. <<PAUSE:short>> So back to our log. The missing mass did not disappear; its atoms floated off invisibly as carbon dioxide and water vapour. Catch those gases and the weight is exactly the same. Remember this and reactions stop being magic: atoms are never made, destroyed, or transformed, they are only rearranged, by breaking old bonds and making new ones. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.narration_chapter: <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:chemistry:chemical_reactions_and_equations:1_2_1:combination_flow>> Drop a little white powder into water, touch the beaker, and your fingers feel heat — no flame, yet the glass is warm. Something just happened inside. That white powder is <<FOCUS:reactant-cao>> calcium oxide, which people call quick lime. <<SECTION:Combination Reaction|id=sec-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> On the left of our story we have two separate things. <<FOCUS:reactant-cao>> Calcium oxide here, and <<FOCUS:reactant-water>> plain water here. <<FOCUS:reactant-cao+reactant-water>> Two reactants, sitting apart, waiting to meet. <<UNFOCUS>> Now watch what happens when they meet. They join together and <<FOCUS:product-caoh2>> become a single new substance. <<WRITE_KEY:Two or more reactants join to form ONE product = combination reaction|id=key-1>> This is the whole idea: <<FOCUS:reactant-cao+reactant-water>> two or more things go in, and exactly <<FOCUS:product-caoh2>> one new product comes out. That is a <<FOCUS:arrow-combine>> combination reaction. <<PAUSE:short>> The one product here is <<FOCUS:product-caoh2>> calcium hydroxide, the substance we call slaked lime. <<UNFOCUS>> Two became one. <<PAUSE:short>> But here is the puzzle: why did the beaker get warm? Nothing was burning, so where did the heat come from? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> When the two reactants lock together into the new product, the rearranging of their atoms <<FOCUS:heat-glyph>> releases stored energy — and that energy escapes as heat. <<WRITE_TEXT:Releases heat = exothermic|id=text-1>> A reaction that gives out heat like this is called exothermic. <<UNFOCUS>> The warm beaker is the proof you can feel. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:reactant-cao+reactant-water>> Calcium oxide plus water combines to give a <<FOCUS:product-caoh2>> single product, calcium hydroxide, and <<FOCUS:heat-glyph>> releases heat. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\text{CaO}(s) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightarrow \text{Ca(OH)}_2(aq) + \text{Heat}|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<UNFOCUS>> So in plain words, calcium oxide plus water gives calcium hydroxide and releases heat. <<WRITE_KEY:Many combination reactions are exothermic|id=key-2>> And this heat is no accident — a great many combination reactions are exothermic, giving out warmth as the new product forms. <<PAUSE:short>> So remember the signature: <<FOCUS:arrow-combine>> count the arrows. If two or more reactants <<FOCUS:product-caoh2>> funnel into a single product, you are looking at a combination reaction — and often, you can feel it happen. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.narration_chapter: <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:chemistry:chemical_reactions_and_equations:1_2_2:decomposition_split>> What if I told you that one single thing, sitting quietly in a dish, can split itself into two completely different things — just because the sun shone on it? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> That white powder is silver chloride, and after a while in sunlight it turns grey. The grey is silver metal, and a greenish gas, chlorine, has quietly slipped away into the air. <<SECTION:Decomposition|id=sec-1>> So one substance became two simpler ones. That is the whole idea of a decomposition reaction: <<FOCUS:parent-compound>> a single substance breaks down into <<FOCUS:product-one+product-two>> two or more simpler substances. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Decomposition = one splits into many|id=text-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> Watch the picture. <<FOCUS:parent-compound>> One block on the left, but on the right it has <<FOCUS:product-one+product-two>> split into two separate blocks. And here is <<FOCUS:product-two>> the second piece. <<FOCUS:parent-compound>> One parent has <<FOCUS:product-one+product-two>> become two children, each simpler than what we started with. <<UNFOCUS>> This is exactly the opposite of a combination reaction, where many things join into one. Here we take one thing and pull it apart. But splitting something apart is hard work. So here is the catch: where does the push to break it come from? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Decomposition needs energy: heat, light, or electricity|id=key-1>> It comes <<FOCUS:energy-arrow+energy-label>> from energy we supply. Every decomposition <<FOCUS:energy-squiggle>> needs energy fed in — and it arrives as heat, as light, or as electricity. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> When the energy is heat, we give it a special name: thermal decomposition. Heat lead nitrate, and one solid crumbles into a solid plus two different gases. With our silver chloride, the energy was light instead. Sunlight alone was enough to tear it into silver and chlorine. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:parent-compound>> Two units of silver chloride, when sunlight is supplied, <<FOCUS:product-one+product-two>> break down into two units of silver metal plus one molecule of chlorine gas. <<WRITE_EQUATION:2AgCl(s) \xrightarrow{\text{sunlight}} 2Ag(s) + Cl_2(g)|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<UNFOCUS>> Here's an example from the chapter. We take solid lead nitrate and heat it strongly. The heat is the energy source that drives this reaction, and our job is to figure out what lead nitrate breaks down into. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Heat solid lead nitrate. What are the products?|id=ex-q-1>> We start by writing the reactant. Solid lead nitrate, written as two P b N O three twice, <<FOCUS:energy-arrow+energy-label>> with heat supplied above the arrow. <<UNFOCUS>> Because a single compound is being split apart by heat, this is a thermal decomposition. <<WRITE_STEP:2Pb(NO3)2 (s) --Heat-->|id=ex-step-1-1>> On heating, the lead nitrate breaks into three products: solid lead oxide, nitrogen dioxide gas, and oxygen gas. <<WRITE_EQUATION:2Pb(NO_3)_2(s) \xrightarrow{\text{Heat}} 2PbO(s) + 4NO_2(g) + O_2(g)|id=ex-eq-1>> So the balanced reaction gives two P b O solid, four N O two gas, and one O two gas. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Products: lead oxide (s) + nitrogen dioxide (g) + oxygen (g)|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. We take about two grams of silver chloride, which starts out white, in a china dish, and we place this dish in sunlight for some time. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: About 2 g of white silver chloride is placed in sunlight. What happens?|id=ex-q-1>> We observe the dish carefully. After being placed in sunlight, the white silver chloride slowly turns grey, and this grey colour is due to the formation of silver metal. <<WRITE_STEP:White silver chloride in sunlight turns grey (silver metal forms)|id=ex-step-1-1>> So light supplies the energy that decomposes the silver chloride, and the products are silver and chlorine gas. The reaction is two A g C l solid, under sunlight, gives two A g solid plus C l two gas. <<WRITE_EQUATION:2AgCl(s) \xrightarrow{Sunlight} 2Ag(s) + Cl_2(g)|id=ex-eq-1>> <<WRITE_ANSWER:Silver chloride decomposes into silver and chlorine gas|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter — the electrolysis of water. We take a plastic mug fitted with two carbon electrodes, and we connect these electrodes to a six volt battery. The mug is filled with water, plus a few drops of dilute sulphuric acid to help conduct the current. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Pass electricity through acidified water and identify the gases produced.|id=ex-q-1>> Now we set up the collection. We take two test tubes filled with water and invert them over the two carbon electrodes. When we switch on the current, we observe the formation of bubbles at both the electrodes, and these bubbles displace the water in the test tubes. <<WRITE_STEP:Bubbles form at both electrodes; gases collect in the two inverted test tubes.|id=ex-step-1-1>> <<PAUSE:short>> Notice carefully: one gas is collected in double the volume of the other — the hydrogen is collected in twice the amount of the oxygen. <<WRITE_STEP:Volume of one gas is double the other (hydrogen = 2 x oxygen).|id=ex-step-1-2>> Finally, we test these gases one by one by bringing a burning candle close to the mouth of the test tubes. The larger volume of gas, the hydrogen, burns with a pop, while the oxygen relights the flame. So acidified water decomposes into hydrogen and oxygen, with hydrogen collected in double the volume of oxygen. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Water decomposes into hydrogen and oxygen; hydrogen is collected in double the volume of oxygen.|id=ex-ans-1>> And if you pass electricity through water, it splits too — into hydrogen and oxygen gas, bubbling off at the two electrodes. <<WRITE_KEY:One substance to many; powered by heat, light or electricity|id=key-2>> So remember the shape of it: one substance breaking down into two or more simpler ones, every time powered by heat, light, or electricity. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.narration_chapter: Drop a shiny iron nail into clear blue copper sulphate solution, wait twenty minutes, and you pull out a nail coated in reddish-brown copper while the blue slowly fades to pale green. <<SECTION:Displacement Reactions|id=sec-1>> Two things changed at once, and that is the whole story: the nail gained a reddish-brown layer, and the blue colour drained away. So here is the honest question: where did that reddish-brown coating come from, and where did the blue colour go? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> The blue colour comes from copper sitting inside the solution, and the reddish-brown coat is that very same copper, now stuck onto the nail. The copper left the solution and landed on the iron. <<WRITE_KEY:More reactive metal displaces less reactive metal from its compound|id=key-1>> And this is the heart of it: a more reactive metal pushes a less reactive metal out of its compound and takes its place. The iron is more reactive, so it shoves the copper out. <<PAUSE:short>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:chemistry:chemical_reactions_and_equations:1_2_3:reactivity_ladder>> To see why iron wins and copper does not, <<FOCUS:reactivity-arrow+reactivity-label>> picture the metals on a ladder, ranked by how reactive they are. <<FOCUS:iron-rung>> Iron sits up here, higher on the ladder, <<FOCUS:copper-rung>> while copper sits lower down. <<UNFOCUS>> Higher means more eager to react. Because iron is above copper, <<TRACE:displacement-direction>> iron can reach down and displace copper from its compound. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Lower metal can't displace higher|id=text-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> But run it the other way: would a copper nail dropped into iron sulphate ever pull the iron out? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> No, nothing happens, because <<FOCUS:copper-rung+iron-rung>> copper is below iron on the ladder. The reactivity series decides the winner, and <<FOCUS:reactivity-arrow>> a lower metal can never displace a higher one. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> Here's an example from the chapter. We take three iron nails and clean them by rubbing with sandpaper. Then we take two test tubes, marked A and B, and in each we pour about ten milliliters of copper sulphate solution, which is a clear blue color. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Why does an iron nail in copper sulphate solution turn brownish while the blue colour fades?|id=ex-q-1>> Iron metal reacts with copper sulphate solution to give iron sulphate solution and solid copper. <<WRITE_EQUATION:Fe(s) + CuSO_4(aq) \rightarrow FeSO_4(aq) + Cu(s)|id=eq-1|boxed>> Now we tie two iron nails together with a thread and immerse them carefully in test tube B for about twenty minutes, while we keep one nail aside for comparison. After twenty minutes, when we take the nails out, the nails turn brownish and the blue color of the solution fades. <<WRITE_STEP:Two nails immersed in test tube B for 20 minutes; one nail kept aside.|id=ex-step-1>> <<WRITE_STEP:Result: nails become brownish, blue colour fades.|id=ex-step-2>> This happens because iron is more reactive than copper, so iron displaces copper from the copper sulphate solution. The reaction is iron plus copper sulphate gives iron sulphate plus copper. The brown coating is the copper deposited on the nail, and the blue fades because the copper sulphate is used up. So the answer is that a displacement reaction takes place. <<WRITE_EQUATION:Fe(s) + CuSO_4(aq) \rightarrow FeSO_4(aq) + Cu(s)|id=ex-eq-1>> <<WRITE_ANSWER:Iron displaces copper: Fe + CuSO4 → FeSO4 + Cu — a displacement reaction.|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. We look at two more displacement reactions. In the first, zinc reacts with copper sulphate. In the second, lead reacts with copper chloride. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Zn + CuSO4 and Pb + CuCl2 — what gets displaced?|id=ex-q-1>> Let's work them out. Zinc plus copper sulphate gives zinc sulphate plus copper. <<WRITE_STEP:Zn(s) + CuSO4(aq) -> ZnSO4(aq) + Cu(s)|id=ex-step-1-1>> And lead plus copper chloride gives lead chloride plus copper. <<WRITE_STEP:Pb(s) + CuCl2(aq) -> PbCl2(aq) + Cu(s)|id=ex-step-1-2>> Why does this happen? Because zinc and lead are more reactive than copper, so each of them pushes copper out of its compound. The answer is that copper is displaced in both reactions. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Zn and Pb, being more reactive than Cu, displace copper from its compounds.|id=ex-ans-1>> Now we can write what actually happened in symbols: iron plus copper sulphate gives iron sulphate plus copper. <<WRITE_KEY:Reactivity series decides who displaces whom|id=key-2>> So remember the whole idea in one line: the higher metal in the reactivity series displaces the lower one out of its compound, and never the reverse. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.narration_chapter: Two perfectly clear liquids. You pour one into the other, and suddenly the mixture turns milky white with a solid settling at the bottom. Nobody added a powder, so where did that solid come from? <<PAUSE:long>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:chemistry:chemical_reactions_and_equations:1_2_4:partner_swap>> <<SECTION:Double Displacement|id=sec-1>> The answer is hiding inside the word displacement, which simply means swapping, and double, which means it happens twice. Think of it like a dance. Each clear liquid holds a compound made of two parts: a positive partner and a negative partner, drifting around dissolved in the water. <<WRITE_TEXT:Each compound = positive part + negative part|id=text-1>> In our case one liquid carries <<FOCUS:sodium-ion+sulphate-ion>> sodium holding hands with sulphate, and the other carries <<FOCUS:barium-ion+chloride-ion>> barium holding hands with chloride. <<UNFOCUS>> Now mix them, and the music starts. <<FOCUS:swap-arrows>> The partners swap: the positive part of one compound goes looking for the negative part of the other. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Double displacement = two compounds swap partners|id=key-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> That is the whole idea: two dissolved compounds trade partners, positive of one joining negative of the other. That is double displacement. <<PAUSE:short>> But here is the twist. <<FOCUS:barium-ion+sulphate-ion>> When barium meets sulphate, the new pair they make refuses to stay dissolved in water. <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> So that brand new barium sulphate pair <<FOCUS:precipitate-solid>> clumps together and sinks. <<UNFOCUS>> That cloudy white solid you saw was created right there in the swap, born from two clear liquids. Meanwhile <<FOCUS:dissolved-product>> sodium and chloride happily pair up too, but they stay spread out and dissolved, invisible in the clear part of the liquid. <<UNFOCUS>> Sodium sulphate plus barium chloride gives barium sulphate, the solid, plus sodium chloride, which stays dissolved. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4(aq) + \text{BaCl}_2(aq) \rightarrow \text{BaSO}_4(s) + 2\text{NaCl}(aq)|id=eq-1|boxed>> An insoluble solid that drops out of a solution like this has a special name: <<FOCUS:precipitate-solid>> a precipitate. <<UNFOCUS>> And any reaction that makes one is called a precipitation reaction. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Insoluble solid that drops out = precipitate|id=key-2>> So whenever a partner swap produces something insoluble, watch for the cloudiness, that solid is your precipitate forming before your eyes. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:aq = dissolved, s = solid precipitate|id=text-2>> Notice the labels: the things that <<FOCUS:dissolved-label>> stay dissolved are marked watery, and <<FOCUS:precipitate-label>> the solid that drops out is marked solid. <<UNFOCUS>> That single label tells you which partner pair became the precipitate. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.narration_chapter: <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:chemistry:chemical_reactions_and_equations:1_2_5:copper_oxygen_exchange>> <<FOCUS:copper-block>> Shiny copper, heated in a china dish, slowly turns jet black. <<UNFOCUS>> Something from the air has crept into the metal. That something <<FOCUS:oxygen-molecule>> is oxygen. <<UNFOCUS>> The air is full of it, and when copper gets hot, the oxygen molecules grab on. <<SECTION:Gaining oxygen|id=sec-1>> Watch <<TRACE:oxygen-arrow-to-copper>> the oxygen move onto the copper. The shiny metal becomes <<FOCUS:copper-oxide-block>> black copper oxide. <<WRITE_KEY:Gains oxygen = oxidised|id=key-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> When a substance gains oxygen during a reaction, we say it has been oxidised. Copper was oxidised to copper oxide. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:copper-block>> Two units of copper combine with <<FOCUS:oxygen-molecule>> one molecule of oxygen gas to give <<FOCUS:copper-oxide-block>> two units of black copper oxide. <<WRITE_EQUATION:2Cu + O_2 \xrightarrow{\text{Heat}} 2CuO|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<UNFOCUS>> So here is a fair question. If gaining oxygen is oxidation, can we ever run this backwards and pull the oxygen back out? <<PAUSE:long>> Yes. <<FOCUS:hydrogen-molecule>> Pass hydrogen gas over the hot black powder, and hydrogen is greedy for oxygen. <<UNFOCUS>> It rips the oxygen straight off the copper oxide. <<PAUSE:short>> <<SECTION:Losing oxygen|id=sec-2>> The <<TRACE:oxygen-arrow-to-hydrogen>> oxygen leaves the copper and joins the hydrogen, <<FOCUS:water-molecule>> forming water. The black coating <<FOCUS:recovered-copper>> turns brown again. <<WRITE_KEY:Loses oxygen = reduced|id=key-2>> <<UNFOCUS>> When a substance loses oxygen, it is reduced. The copper oxide lost its oxygen, so it was reduced back to copper. <<PAUSE:short>> Copper oxide plus hydrogen gives copper plus water, as <<TRACE:oxygen-arrow-to-hydrogen>> the oxygen moves from the copper to the hydrogen. <<WRITE_EQUATION:CuO + H_2 \xrightarrow{\text{Heat}} Cu + H_2O|id=eq-2|boxed>> <<UNFOCUS>> Now look closely at the same reaction. The <<FOCUS:copper-oxide-block>> copper oxide lost oxygen, but the <<FOCUS:hydrogen-molecule>> hydrogen gained it. <<WRITE_KEY:One oxidised, one reduced, together|id=key-3>> <<UNFOCUS>> So in one single reaction, one reactant is reduced while the other is oxidised, at the very same time. They always come as a pair. <<PAUSE:short>> Here's an example from the chapter. We take about one gram of copper powder and heat it in a china dish. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Heat about 1 g copper powder in a china dish. Why does its surface turn black?|id=ex-q-1>> As the copper powder is heated, its surface becomes coated with a black substance. That black coating is copper two oxide, because oxygen from the air is added to the copper. <<WRITE_STEP:Surface becomes coated with black copper(II) oxide|id=ex-step-1-1>> So the reaction is this: two copper plus one oxygen gas, on heating, gives two copper oxide. Oxygen is added to copper, and that addition of oxygen is exactly what we call oxidation. <<WRITE_EQUATION:2Cu + O_2 \xrightarrow{\text{Heat}} 2CuO|id=ex-eq-1>> <<WRITE_ANSWER:Copper is oxidised to black copper(II) oxide: 2Cu + O2 → 2CuO|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. When hydrogen gas is passed over heated copper oxide, the black coating on the surface turns brown as copper is obtained. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Hydrogen gas is passed over heated copper oxide. What happens?|id=ex-q-1>> Let's write the reaction. Copper oxide plus hydrogen gives copper plus water. <<WRITE_STEP:CuO + H2 (heat) -> Cu + H2O|id=ex-step-1-1>> Now look closely at what each substance does. The copper oxide loses oxygen, so the copper oxide is reduced. <<WRITE_STEP:Copper oxide loses oxygen -> reduced|id=ex-step-1-2>> Meanwhile the hydrogen gains that oxygen to form water, so the hydrogen is oxidised. Reduction and oxidation happen together. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Copper oxide is reduced; hydrogen is oxidised - a redox reaction|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. Consider this reaction: zinc oxide plus carbon gives zinc plus carbon monoxide. Let's figure out which substance is oxidised and which is reduced. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: In ZnO + C -> Zn + CO, identify what is oxidised and what is reduced|id=ex-q-1>> First, look at the carbon. Carbon starts on its own and ends up combined with oxygen as carbon monoxide. Since carbon gains oxygen, carbon is oxidised to carbon monoxide. <<WRITE_STEP:Carbon gains oxygen, so carbon is oxidised to carbon monoxide|id=ex-step-1-1>> Now look at the zinc oxide. It begins with oxygen attached and ends as plain zinc, having lost that oxygen. Since zinc oxide loses oxygen, zinc oxide is reduced to zinc. <<WRITE_STEP:Zinc oxide loses oxygen, so zinc oxide is reduced to zinc|id=ex-step-1-2>> So in this reaction, carbon is oxidised to carbon monoxide, and zinc oxide is reduced to zinc. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Carbon is oxidised to carbon monoxide; zinc oxide is reduced to zinc|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. Consider the reaction where manganese dioxide plus four hydrochloric acid gives manganese chloride plus two water plus chlorine. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Identify oxidation and reduction in MnO2 + 4HCl -> MnCl2 + 2H2O + Cl2|id=ex-q-1>> Let's look at what happens to each species. The hydrochloric acid is oxidised to chlorine, because it loses electrons and gains oxygen character as it forms chlorine gas. <<WRITE_STEP:Hydrochloric acid is oxidised to chlorine|id=ex-step-1-1>> <<WRITE_EQUATION:MnO_2 + 4HCl \rightarrow MnCl_2 + 2H_2O + Cl_2|id=ex-eq-1>> At the same time, the manganese dioxide is reduced to manganese chloride, because it loses oxygen and gains electrons. So we have both oxidation and reduction in the same reaction. <<WRITE_STEP:Manganese dioxide is reduced to manganese chloride|id=ex-step-1-2>> <<WRITE_ANSWER:Hydrochloric acid is oxidised to chlorine; manganese dioxide is reduced to manganese chloride|id=ex-ans-1>> Because both happen together, we give the whole thing one name. We call it a redox reaction, short for reduction and oxidation. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Oxygen handed off: one gains, one loses|id=text-1>> So remember the picture: oxygen gets handed from one substance to another. Whoever takes it is oxidised, whoever gives it up is reduced, and the swap is redox.

segments.narration_chapter: <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:chemistry:chemical_reactions_and_equations:1_3_1:corrosion_three_metals>> Leave a shiny new iron nail outside for a few weeks, and it comes back covered in a flaky, reddish-brown powder. Something has been quietly eating it. Here's the <<FOCUS:iron-nail-shiny+iron-nail-rusted>> same nail before and after. segments.narration_chapter: Open a packet of chips that's been sitting in the cupboard for months, and it hits you — that stale, almost paint-like smell. What actually happened to those chips? Something quieter happened — the oxygen in the air slowly attacked the oil they were fried in. <<SECTION:Rancidity|id=sec-1>> Fats and oils react with oxygen from the air in a chemical reaction. That single word, rancidity, is the whole story. <<PAUSE:short>> Here's the honest question, though: if it's just oxygen doing this, why doesn't every packet of chips on the shelf taste terrible the day you buy it? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> Because oxidation is slow, and manufacturers fight it. The trick is simple — if oxygen causes rancidity, then take the oxygen away. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_STEP:Air-tight containers limit oxygen contact|id=step-1>> That's why oily food is sealed in air-tight containers — less air touching the fat means slower oxidation. <<WRITE_STEP:Antioxidants are added to react with oxygen first|id=step-2>> It's also why packets list antioxidants. These are substances that get oxidised instead of the fat, taking the hit so the oil stays fresh. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_STEP:Chip bags flushed with nitrogen, not air|id=step-3>> And the cleverest trick — chip manufacturers flush the bag with nitrogen gas. Nitrogen is unreactive, so with no oxygen inside, the chips simply can't go rancid. <<PAUSE:short>> Squeeze a sealed chip packet and feel how puffy it is. That cushion isn't air — it's nitrogen, quietly protecting your snack. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:No oxygen, no rancidity|id=key-2>> So next time food smells off, you'll know the culprit: oxygen oxidising the fats and oils.
