lesson_plans.title: Word Equations: The Shorthand of Chemistry

hook.text: Imagine a thin strip of metal that bursts into a blinding white flame, and when the light dies, all that's left is a little heap of white powder. What just happened?

crucial_facts: A chemical reaction turns reactants into a new product, and we write it as reactants on the left, an arrow, and products on the right.
The arrow means 'turns into' and always points from reactants towards products.

diagrams.purpose: Show the structure of a word equation: reactants on the left, arrow in the middle, product on the right, so the student sees WHY each piece sits where it does.

required_elements.description: The word 'Magnesium' written on the left-hand side as the first reactant.
A plus sign between the two reactants on the left.
The word 'Oxygen' written on the left-hand side as the second reactant.
A large arrow pointing from left to right, sitting between the reactants and the product.
The words 'Magnesium oxide' written on the right-hand side as the product.
A brace or bracket under Magnesium and Oxygen labelled 'Reactants'.
A brace or bracket under Magnesium oxide labelled 'Product'.

choreography.narration: Imagine a thin strip of metal that bursts into a blinding white flame, and when the light dies, all that's left is a little heap of white powder.
That strip is magnesium ribbon, and that white powder is something brand new called magnesium oxide. The magnesium grabbed oxygen out of the air and became a completely different substance.
<<SECTION:Describing a reaction|id=sec-1>>So how do we describe what happened? You could say a whole sentence: when magnesium ribbon is burnt in oxygen, it gets converted to magnesium oxide.
That's correct, but imagine writing a paragraph like that every single time you wanted to talk about a reaction. Wouldn't you want a shorter way?
Chemists did exactly that. They invented a shorthand, and the simplest version is called a word equation.
<<WRITE_TEXT:Word equation = shorthand for a reaction|id=text-1>>Here's the idea. The stuff you start with goes on the left. We start with magnesium, and we start with oxygen.
Because there are two starting substances, we join them with a plus sign, just like adding ingredients in a recipe.
These starting substances have a special name. We call them the reactants, the things that react.
Now, the magnesium and oxygen turn into something new. We show 'turns into' with an arrow, and the arrowhead points the way the reaction goes.
<<WRITE_KEY:Reactants, then arrow, then product|id=key-1>>And where the arrow points, on the right-hand side, we write the new substance that's made: magnesium oxide. That's the product.

Here's an example from the chapter. When we burn a magnesium ribbon in oxygen, it produces magnesium oxide. The substances that take part, magnesium and oxygen, are the reactants, and the new substance formed, magnesium oxide, is the product. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Write the word-equation for burning magnesium ribbon in oxygen.|id=ex-q-1>>

We start by placing the reactants on the left-hand side. Magnesium and oxygen are what we begin with, so we write magnesium plus oxygen on the left. <<WRITE_STEP:Magnesium + Oxygen (reactants, left-hand side)|id=ex-step-1-1>>

Next we draw an arrow pointing toward the product, and on the right-hand side we write the product, magnesium oxide. The arrow shows the direction of the reaction, from reactants to product. <<WRITE_STEP:Magnesium + Oxygen → Magnesium oxide|id=ex-step-1-2>>
And so the complete word-equation is: magnesium plus oxygen gives magnesium oxide. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Magnesium + Oxygen → Magnesium oxide|id=ex-ans-1>>
Look at the whole thing now: magnesium plus oxygen, arrow, magnesium oxide. Reactants on the left, the new product on the right.
So remember this shape: reactants on the left, an arrow that means 'turns into' pointing right, and the products on the right. That single line tells the whole story of the reaction.

lesson_plans.title: Writing a Chemical Equation

hook.text: Strike a ribbon of magnesium and it flares with a blinding white light — but how do you write down what just happened without scribbling a whole sentence?

crucial_facts: A chemical equation uses formulae and an arrow to show reactants on the left turning into products on the right.
Each substance is written as its chemical formula, like Mg, O two, and M g O — not as its name in words.

diagrams.purpose: Show the transformation from a clumsy word sentence into a compact symbolic equation, making clear what the arrow, the left side, and the right side each mean.

required_elements.description: The word sentence: 'magnesium plus oxygen gives magnesium oxide' written across the top.
The left-hand side of the symbolic equation showing Mg + O2.
A right-pointing arrow between the two sides, meaning 'turns into'.
The right-hand side of the symbolic equation showing MgO.
The formula Mg for magnesium on the left side.
The formula O2 for oxygen gas on the left side.
The formula MgO for magnesium oxide on the right side.

choreography.narration: Strike a ribbon of magnesium and it flares with a blinding white light — but how do you write down what just happened without scribbling a whole sentence?
In words you'd say: magnesium reacts with oxygen to give magnesium oxide. True, but long and clumsy — and imagine writing that for every reaction.
<<SECTION:Writing a Chemical Equation|id=sec-1>>So chemists found a shorter, smarter way: instead of spelling out names, they swap in each substance's chemical formula.
Magnesium is simply Mg. Oxygen in the air travels as a pair of atoms locked together, so we write it as O two. And magnesium oxide is M g O.
Now here's the real question: where do these formulae go, and what holds the whole thing together?
The substances you start with — magnesium and oxygen — go on the left. We call them the reactants.
Then we draw an arrow pointing right. Read that arrow as the words 'turns into' — it shows the direction the reaction goes.
And on the right side goes what you end up with: magnesium oxide, the product.
<<WRITE_KEY:Equation: reactants (left) arrow products (right), all as formulae|id=key-1>>Put it together and the whole reaction collapses into one tidy line: Mg plus O two, arrow, M g O.

<<WRITE_TEXT:Skeletal equation = formulae only, not yet checked|id=text-1>>This compact form, written straight from the formulae, is called a skeletal chemical equation — the bare bones of the reaction.
One quiet thing to notice: oxygen had to be written as O two, not just O, because that's how it actually exists in the air — as pairs of atoms.
So a long sentence became a single symbolic line: formulae for the substances, an arrow for 'turns into', reactants on the left and products on the right. That's a chemical equation.

equations.explanation_in_words: Magnesium plus oxygen, arrow meaning turns into, gives magnesium oxide.

lesson_plans.title: Balanced Chemical Equations

hook.text: If you weigh a closed jar before and after a reaction happens inside it, the needle on the scale does not move even a hair. Where did the new stuff come from?

crucial_facts: The number of atoms of each element must be exactly the same on both sides of the equation, because atoms are never created or destroyed.
We balance only by changing the big numbers in front of the formulas, never the small subscripts inside them.

diagrams.purpose: Show reactant atoms equalling product atoms so conservation of mass becomes visible as a literal count.

required_elements.description: Left side of the equation showing the reactant molecules as clusters of coloured atom circles.
Right side of the equation showing the product molecules as clusters of coloured atom circles.
Reaction arrow pointing from reactants to products in the middle.
A small running tally listing how many atoms of each element sit on the reactant side.
A small running tally listing how many atoms of each element sit on the product side.
A highlighted big number that can be placed in front of a formula to multiply its whole cluster.
A locked padlock icon sitting on a subscript inside a formula, marking it as untouchable.

choreography.narration: If you weigh a sealed jar before and after a reaction fizzes away inside it, the scale does not move even a hair. So where does the new stuff come from?
The answer is that nothing new is ever made. The atoms you start with are the exact same atoms you finish with, just rearranged into new partners.
<<SECTION:Conservation of mass|id=sec-1>>This is the law of conservation of mass you met last year. Mass can neither be created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction.

<<WRITE_KEY:Atoms in equals atoms out, for every element|id=key-1>>Said in plain terms, the number of atoms of each element stays exactly the same before and after. Count them on the left, count them on the right, and the two counts must match.
Watch how we check this. On the reactant side I tally up each kind of atom one element at a time.
Now the product side. If every element's tally on the right matches the left, the equation is already balanced.
But what happens when a count does not match? Say there are four oxygen atoms on one side but only one on the other. Can we just shrink the formula?
No. The little subscript numbers inside a formula are locked. Changing water from H two O to H O would turn it into a completely different substance.
Instead, we place a big number in front of the whole formula. That number multiplies every atom in the cluster at once, like buying two identical boxes instead of repacking one.
<<WRITE_STEP:Adjust front coefficients until both tallies match|id=step-1>>We keep adjusting those front numbers until the reactant tally and the product tally agree for every single element.
<<WRITE_TEXT:Big numbers in front, never the small subscripts|id=text-1>>So the whole method is just bookkeeping for atoms. Change the big numbers in front, never the small subscripts inside.
And when both tallies finally match, every atom is accounted for, the mass is conserved, and the scale on that sealed jar stays perfectly still.

equations.latex: \text{atoms of each element}_{\text{reactants}} = \text{atoms of each element}_{\text{products}}
equations.explanation_in_words: For every element, the number of atoms on the reactant side equals the number of atoms on the product side.
Here is a reaction where zinc meets sulphuric acid to give zinc sulphate and hydrogen, and the count already matches on both sides.

lesson_plans.title: What Actually Changes in a Chemical Reaction

hook.text: Burn a log to ash and the ash weighs less, yet not a single atom was destroyed. So where did the missing stuff go?

crucial_facts: In a chemical reaction atoms are never created, destroyed, or changed into other kinds of atoms; they are only rearranged.
A chemical reaction is the breaking of old bonds and the making of new ones, which is why the same atoms become brand-new substances.

diagrams.purpose: Show the same atoms before and after a reaction, with old bonds breaking and new bonds forming, so the student sees rearrangement rather than creation or destruction.

required_elements.description: Two hydrogen atoms bonded as one molecule and two oxygen atoms bonded as one molecule, on the left, labelled reactants.
The bonds inside the reactant molecules, drawn as lines, that will break.
Two water molecules on the right, each made of the very same atoms now arranged differently, labelled products.
The new bonds inside the water molecules that form during the reaction.
A small tally showing the atom count of each element is identical on both sides.

choreography.narration: Burn a log down to a pile of ash, weigh it, and the ash is lighter than the log you started with. Yet chemistry insists not one atom was destroyed.
So where did the missing mass go? Hold that question, because the answer rewrites what you think a reaction even is.

<<SECTION:Atoms are stubborn|id=sec-1>>Here is the first stubborn rule. During an ordinary chemical reaction, an atom of oxygen stays an atom of oxygen. It never becomes carbon, never becomes anything else.
And atoms never vanish into nothing, and they never appear from nowhere. Whatever you started with, you still have, every last one.
But if the atoms are all the same and all still here, then how on earth do we get a brand-new substance out the other side?
Watch the lines holding these atoms together. Those lines are bonds, and as the reaction begins, the old bonds break apart.
<<WRITE_KEY:Reaction = break old bonds, make new bonds|id=key-1>>Now the very same atoms link up in a new pattern, and fresh bonds form. The atoms are old; the arrangement is new.
And there is your new substance. Same building blocks, a different structure. That is the whole secret of a chemical reaction.
<<WRITE_TEXT:Same atoms, new arrangement|id=text-1>>Count them. Every kind of atom appears exactly as many times on the right as it did on the left. Nothing gained, nothing lost.
So back to our log. The missing mass did not disappear; its atoms floated off invisibly as carbon dioxide and water vapour. Catch those gases and the weight is exactly the same.
Remember this and reactions stop being magic: atoms are never made, destroyed, or transformed, they are only rearranged, by breaking old bonds and making new ones.

lesson_plans.title: Combination Reactions: Two Become One

hook.text: Drop a little white powder into water, touch the beaker, and your fingers feel heat — no flame, no fire, yet the glass is warm. Something just combined.

crucial_facts: A combination reaction is one where two or more reactants join to form a single new product.
Many combination reactions release heat — they are exothermic.

diagrams.purpose: Show two reactants merging into a single product, making the 'two in, one out' pattern visual and memorable.

required_elements.description: A box on the left labelled calcium oxide (quick lime), the white powder.
A second box on the left labelled water.
A plus sign between the two reactant boxes.
A large arrow pointing right from the two reactants toward the single product, with a small heat/flame glyph beside it.
A single box on the right labelled calcium hydroxide (slaked lime), the one new product.
A small heat-wave or warmth symbol near the arrow showing heat is released.

choreography.narration: Drop a little white powder into water, touch the beaker, and your fingers feel heat — no flame, yet the glass is warm. Something just happened inside.
That white powder is calcium oxide, which people call quick lime. <<SECTION:Combination Reaction|id=sec-1>>On the left of our story we have two separate things.
Calcium oxide here, and plain water here. Two reactants, sitting apart, waiting to meet.
Now watch what happens when they meet. They join together and become a single new substance.

<<WRITE_KEY:Two or more reactants join to form ONE product = combination reaction|id=key-1>>This is the whole idea: two or more things go in, and exactly one new product comes out. That is a combination reaction.
The one product here is calcium hydroxide, the substance we call slaked lime. Two became one.
But here is the puzzle: why did the beaker get warm? Nothing was burning, so where did the heat come from?
When the two reactants lock together into the new product, the rearranging of their atoms releases stored energy — and that energy escapes as heat.
<<WRITE_TEXT:Releases heat = exothermic|id=text-1>>A reaction that gives out heat like this is called exothermic. The warm beaker is the proof you can feel.
So in plain words, calcium oxide plus water gives calcium hydroxide and releases heat.
<<WRITE_KEY:Many combination reactions are exothermic|id=key-2>>And this heat is no accident — a great many combination reactions are exothermic, giving out warmth as the new product forms.
So remember the signature: count the arrows. If two or more reactants funnel into a single product, you are looking at a combination reaction — and often, you can feel it happen.

equations.explanation_in_words: Calcium oxide plus water combines to give a single product, calcium hydroxide, and releases heat.

lesson_plans.title: Decomposition: One Becomes Many

hook.text: What if I told you that one single thing, sitting quietly in a dish, can split itself into two completely different things — just because the sun shone on it?

crucial_facts: In a decomposition reaction, one substance breaks down into two or more simpler substances.
Decomposition always needs energy supplied — as heat, light, or electricity.

diagrams.purpose: Show one compound splitting into multiple simpler products, contrasting visually with combination, and showing the energy input that drives it.

required_elements.description: A single labelled block representing one starting compound, for example AB, sitting on the left.
A bold arrow from the parent compound to the products, labelled with the energy source (heat, light, or electricity).
First simpler product, labelled A, on the right.
Second simpler product, labelled B, on the right, below product-one.

choreography.narration: What if I told you that one single thing, sitting quietly in a dish, can split itself into two completely different things — just because the sun shone on it?
That white powder is silver chloride, and after a while in sunlight it turns grey. The grey is silver metal, and a greenish gas, chlorine, has quietly slipped away into the air.
<<SECTION:Decomposition|id=sec-1>>So one substance became two simpler ones. That is the whole idea of a decomposition reaction: a single substance breaks down into two or more simpler substances.
<<WRITE_TEXT:Decomposition = one splits into many|id=text-1>>Watch the picture. One block on the left, but on the right it has split into two separate blocks.
And here is the second piece. One parent has become two children, each simpler than what we started with.
This is exactly the opposite of a combination reaction, where many things join into one. Here we take one thing and pull it apart.
But splitting something apart is hard work. So here is the catch: where does the push to break it come from?

<<WRITE_KEY:Decomposition needs energy: heat, light, or electricity|id=key-1>>It comes from energy we supply. Every decomposition needs energy fed in — and it arrives as heat, as light, or as electricity.
When the energy is heat, we give it a special name: thermal decomposition. Heat lead nitrate, and one solid crumbles into a solid plus two different gases.
With our silver chloride, the energy was light instead. Sunlight alone was enough to tear it into silver and chlorine.

Here's an example from the chapter. We take solid lead nitrate and heat it strongly. The heat is the energy source that drives this reaction, and our job is to figure out what lead nitrate breaks down into. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Heat solid lead nitrate. What are the products?|id=ex-q-1>>

We start by writing the reactant. Solid lead nitrate, written as two P b N O three twice, with heat supplied above the arrow. Because a single compound is being split apart by heat, this is a thermal decomposition. <<WRITE_STEP:2Pb(NO3)2 (s) --Heat-->|id=ex-step-1-1>>

On heating, the lead nitrate breaks into three products: solid lead oxide, nitrogen dioxide gas, and oxygen gas. <<WRITE_EQUATION:2Pb(NO_3)_2(s) \xrightarrow{\text{Heat}} 2PbO(s) + 4NO_2(g) + O_2(g)|id=ex-eq-1>> So the balanced reaction gives two P b O solid, four N O two gas, and one O two gas. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Products: lead oxide (s) + nitrogen dioxide (g) + oxygen (g)|id=ex-ans-1>>

Here's an example from the chapter. We take about two grams of silver chloride, which starts out white, in a china dish, and we place this dish in sunlight for some time. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: About 2 g of white silver chloride is placed in sunlight. What happens?|id=ex-q-1>>

We observe the dish carefully. After being placed in sunlight, the white silver chloride slowly turns grey, and this grey colour is due to the formation of silver metal. <<WRITE_STEP:White silver chloride in sunlight turns grey (silver metal forms)|id=ex-step-1-1>>

So light supplies the energy that decomposes the silver chloride, and the products are silver and chlorine gas. The reaction is two A g C l solid, under sunlight, gives two A g solid plus C l two gas. <<WRITE_EQUATION:2AgCl(s) \xrightarrow{Sunlight} 2Ag(s) + Cl_2(g)|id=ex-eq-1>> <<WRITE_ANSWER:Silver chloride decomposes into silver and chlorine gas|id=ex-ans-1>>

Here's an example from the chapter — the electrolysis of water. We take a plastic mug fitted with two carbon electrodes, and we connect these electrodes to a six volt battery. The mug is filled with water, plus a few drops of dilute sulphuric acid to help conduct the current. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Pass electricity through acidified water and identify the gases produced.|id=ex-q-1>>

Now we set up the collection. We take two test tubes filled with water and invert them over the two carbon electrodes. When we switch on the current, we observe the formation of bubbles at both the electrodes, and these bubbles displace the water in the test tubes. <<WRITE_STEP:Bubbles form at both electrodes; gases collect in the two inverted test tubes.|id=ex-step-1-1>><<PAUSE:short>> Notice carefully: one gas is collected in double the volume of the other — the hydrogen is collected in twice the amount of the oxygen. <<WRITE_STEP:Volume of one gas is double the other (hydrogen = 2 x oxygen).|id=ex-step-1-2>>

Finally, we test these gases one by one by bringing a burning candle close to the mouth of the test tubes. The larger volume of gas, the hydrogen, burns with a pop, while the oxygen relights the flame. So acidified water decomposes into hydrogen and oxygen, with hydrogen collected in double the volume of oxygen. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Water decomposes into hydrogen and oxygen; hydrogen is collected in double the volume of oxygen.|id=ex-ans-1>>
And if you pass electricity through water, it splits too — into hydrogen and oxygen gas, bubbling off at the two electrodes.

<<WRITE_KEY:One substance to many; powered by heat, light or electricity|id=key-2>>So remember the shape of it: one substance breaking down into two or more simpler ones, every time powered by heat, light, or electricity.

equations.explanation_in_words: Two units of silver chloride, when sunlight is supplied, break down into two units of silver metal plus one molecule of chlorine gas.

lesson_plans.title: Displacement Reactions: When One Metal Kicks Out Another

hook.text: Drop a shiny iron nail into clear blue copper sulphate solution, wait twenty minutes, and you pull out a nail coated in reddish-brown copper while the blue slowly fades to pale green.

crucial_facts: In a displacement reaction, a more reactive metal pushes a less reactive metal out of its compound and takes its place.
Whether displacement happens is decided by the reactivity series: the higher metal displaces the lower one, never the other way around.

diagrams.purpose: Show the reactivity series as a ladder so the student can see that iron sits above copper, which is exactly why iron can displace copper but copper cannot displace iron.

required_elements.description: A rung labelled 'Iron' positioned higher up the ladder, marked as more reactive.
A rung labelled 'Copper' positioned lower on the ladder, marked as less reactive.
A vertical arrow along the ladder pointing upward, labelled 'increasing reactivity'.
A curved arrow from iron-rung pointing down to copper-rung, showing the direction in which displacement is allowed.

choreography.narration: Drop a shiny iron nail into clear blue copper sulphate solution, wait twenty minutes, and you pull out a nail coated in reddish-brown copper while the blue slowly fades to pale green.
<<SECTION:Displacement Reactions|id=sec-1>>Two things changed at once, and that is the whole story: the nail gained a reddish-brown layer, and the blue colour drained away.
So here is the honest question: where did that reddish-brown coating come from, and where did the blue colour go?
The blue colour comes from copper sitting inside the solution, and the reddish-brown coat is that very same copper, now stuck onto the nail. The copper left the solution and landed on the iron.

<<WRITE_KEY:More reactive metal displaces less reactive metal from its compound|id=key-1>>And this is the heart of it: a more reactive metal pushes a less reactive metal out of its compound and takes its place. The iron is more reactive, so it shoves the copper out.
To see why iron wins and copper does not, picture the metals on a ladder, ranked by how reactive they are.
Iron sits up here, higher on the ladder, while copper sits lower down. Higher means more eager to react.
Because iron is above copper, iron can reach down and displace copper from its compound.
<<WRITE_TEXT:Lower metal can't displace higher|id=text-1>>But run it the other way: would a copper nail dropped into iron sulphate ever pull the iron out?
No, nothing happens, because copper is below iron on the ladder. The reactivity series decides the winner, and a lower metal can never displace a higher one.

Here's an example from the chapter. We take three iron nails and clean them by rubbing with sandpaper. Then we take two test tubes, marked A and B, and in each we pour about ten milliliters of copper sulphate solution, which is a clear blue color. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Why does an iron nail in copper sulphate solution turn brownish while the blue colour fades?|id=ex-q-1>>

Now we tie two iron nails together with a thread and immerse them carefully in test tube B for about twenty minutes, while we keep one nail aside for comparison. After twenty minutes, when we take the nails out, the nails turn brownish and the blue color of the solution fades. <<WRITE_STEP:Two nails immersed in test tube B for 20 minutes; one nail kept aside.|id=ex-step-1>> <<WRITE_STEP:Result: nails become brownish, blue colour fades.|id=ex-step-2>>

This happens because iron is more reactive than copper, so iron displaces copper from the copper sulphate solution. The reaction is iron plus copper sulphate gives iron sulphate plus copper. The brown coating is the copper deposited on the nail, and the blue fades because the copper sulphate is used up. So the answer is that a displacement reaction takes place. <<WRITE_EQUATION:Fe(s) + CuSO_4(aq) \rightarrow FeSO_4(aq) + Cu(s)|id=ex-eq-1>> <<WRITE_ANSWER:Iron displaces copper: Fe + CuSO4 → FeSO4 + Cu — a displacement reaction.|id=ex-ans-1>>

Here's an example from the chapter. We look at two more displacement reactions. In the first, zinc reacts with copper sulphate. In the second, lead reacts with copper chloride. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Zn + CuSO4 and Pb + CuCl2 — what gets displaced?|id=ex-q-1>>

Let's work them out. Zinc plus copper sulphate gives zinc sulphate plus copper. <<WRITE_STEP:Zn(s) + CuSO4(aq) -> ZnSO4(aq) + Cu(s)|id=ex-step-1-1>> And lead plus copper chloride gives lead chloride plus copper. <<WRITE_STEP:Pb(s) + CuCl2(aq) -> PbCl2(aq) + Cu(s)|id=ex-step-1-2>>

Why does this happen? Because zinc and lead are more reactive than copper, so each of them pushes copper out of its compound. The answer is that copper is displaced in both reactions. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Zn and Pb, being more reactive than Cu, displace copper from its compounds.|id=ex-ans-1>>
Now we can write what actually happened in symbols: iron plus copper sulphate gives iron sulphate plus copper.

<<WRITE_KEY:Reactivity series decides who displaces whom|id=key-2>>So remember the whole idea in one line: the higher metal in the reactivity series displaces the lower one out of its compound, and never the reverse.

equations.explanation_in_words: Iron metal reacts with copper sulphate solution to give iron sulphate solution and solid copper.

lesson_plans.title: Double Displacement: The Partner Swap That Drops a Solid

hook.text: Two perfectly clear liquids. You pour one into the other... and suddenly the mixture turns cloudy white, with a solid sinking to the bottom. Nobody added a powder. Where did it come from?

crucial_facts: In a double displacement reaction, two dissolved compounds swap partners: the positive part of one joins the negative part of the other.
When the swap produces an insoluble solid, that solid is called a precipitate, and the reaction is a precipitation reaction.

diagrams.purpose: Show two dissolved compounds, each made of a positive and negative part, swapping partners so one new pair drops out as an insoluble solid.

required_elements.description: A blue circle labelled sodium (Na, positive), one of two starting partners, floating in solution.
A green circle labelled sulphate (SO4, negative), originally paired with sodium.
An orange circle labelled barium (Ba, positive), originally paired with chloride.
A purple circle labelled chloride (Cl, negative), originally paired with barium.
Two crossing arrows showing the partner swap: barium reaching toward sulphate, sodium reaching toward chloride.
A solid white clump formed when barium joins sulphate, drawn sinking to the bottom as the insoluble precipitate.
Sodium and chloride paired but still shown dissolved and spread out in the liquid, staying in solution.

choreography.narration: Two perfectly clear liquids. You pour one into the other, and suddenly the mixture turns milky white with a solid settling at the bottom. Nobody added a powder, so where did that solid come from?
<<SECTION:Double Displacement|id=sec-1>>The answer is hiding inside the word displacement, which simply means swapping, and double, which means it happens twice.
Think of it like a dance. Each clear liquid holds a compound made of two parts: a positive partner and a negative partner, drifting around dissolved in the water.
<<WRITE_TEXT:Each compound = positive part + negative part|id=text-1>>In our case one liquid carries sodium holding hands with sulphate, and the other carries barium holding hands with chloride.
Now mix them, and the music starts. The partners swap: the positive part of one compound goes looking for the negative part of the other.

<<WRITE_KEY:Double displacement = two compounds swap partners|id=key-1>>That is the whole idea: two dissolved compounds trade partners, positive of one joining negative of the other. That is double displacement.
But here is the twist. When barium meets sulphate, the new pair they make refuses to stay dissolved in water.
So that brand new barium sulphate pair clumps together and sinks. That cloudy white solid you saw was created right there in the swap, born from two clear liquids.
Meanwhile sodium and chloride happily pair up too, but they stay spread out and dissolved, invisible in the clear part of the liquid.
An insoluble solid that drops out of a solution like this has a special name: a precipitate. And any reaction that makes one is called a precipitation reaction.

<<WRITE_KEY:Insoluble solid that drops out = precipitate|id=key-2>>So whenever a partner swap produces something insoluble, watch for the cloudiness, that solid is your precipitate forming before your eyes.

<<WRITE_TEXT:aq = dissolved, s = solid precipitate|id=text-2>>Notice the labels: the things that stay dissolved are marked watery, and the solid that drops out is marked solid. That single label tells you which partner pair became the precipitate.

equations.explanation_in_words: Sodium sulphate plus barium chloride gives barium sulphate, the solid, plus sodium chloride, which stays dissolved.

lesson_plans.title: Oxidation and Reduction: The Oxygen Tug-of-War

hook.text: Shiny copper, heated in a dish, slowly turns jet black. Heat it the right way again, and the black peels back to copper. Two reactions, mirror images of each other.

crucial_facts: A substance is oxidised when it gains oxygen, and reduced when it loses oxygen.
In every redox reaction one reactant is oxidised while the other is reduced, at the same time.

diagrams.purpose: Show oxygen being handed from air to copper (oxidation) and then handed from copper oxide to hydrogen (reduction), making the tug-of-war visible.

required_elements.description: A shiny orange-brown block of copper labelled Cu on the left.
An oxygen molecule from the air, shown as two joined red circles labelled O2, above the copper.
A black block labelled CuO, the result of copper gaining oxygen.
An arrow showing oxygen moving from the air onto the copper, annotated oxidised.
A hydrogen molecule labelled H2 on the right side, brought in for the reverse reaction.
A water molecule labelled H2O formed when hydrogen takes the oxygen.
An arrow showing oxygen leaving copper oxide and joining hydrogen, annotated reduced.
A brown block of copper recovered after copper oxide loses its oxygen.

choreography.narration: Shiny copper, heated in a china dish, slowly turns jet black. Something from the air has crept into the metal.
That something is oxygen. The air is full of it, and when copper gets hot, the oxygen molecules grab on.
<<SECTION:Gaining oxygen|id=sec-1>>Watch the oxygen move onto the copper. The shiny metal becomes black copper oxide.
<<WRITE_KEY:Gains oxygen = oxidised|id=key-1>>When a substance gains oxygen during a reaction, we say it has been oxidised. Copper was oxidised to copper oxide.
So here is a fair question. If gaining oxygen is oxidation, can we ever run this backwards and pull the oxygen back out?
Yes. Pass hydrogen gas over the hot black powder, and hydrogen is greedy for oxygen. It rips the oxygen straight off the copper oxide.
<<SECTION:Losing oxygen|id=sec-2>>The oxygen leaves the copper and joins the hydrogen, forming water. The black coating turns brown again.
<<WRITE_KEY:Loses oxygen = reduced|id=key-2>>When a substance loses oxygen, it is reduced. The copper oxide lost its oxygen, so it was reduced back to copper.
Now look closely at the same reaction. The copper oxide lost oxygen, but the hydrogen gained it.
<<WRITE_KEY:One oxidised, one reduced, together|id=key-3>>So in one single reaction, one reactant is reduced while the other is oxidised, at the very same time. They always come as a pair.

Here's an example from the chapter. We take about one gram of copper powder and heat it in a china dish. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Heat about 1 g copper powder in a china dish. Why does its surface turn black?|id=ex-q-1>>

As the copper powder is heated, its surface becomes coated with a black substance. That black coating is copper two oxide, because oxygen from the air is added to the copper. <<WRITE_STEP:Surface becomes coated with black copper(II) oxide|id=ex-step-1-1>>

So the reaction is this: two copper plus one oxygen gas, on heating, gives two copper oxide. Oxygen is added to copper, and that addition of oxygen is exactly what we call oxidation. <<WRITE_EQUATION:2Cu + O_2 \xrightarrow{\text{Heat}} 2CuO|id=ex-eq-1>><<WRITE_ANSWER:Copper is oxidised to black copper(II) oxide: 2Cu + O2 → 2CuO|id=ex-ans-1>>

Here's an example from the chapter. When hydrogen gas is passed over heated copper oxide, the black coating on the surface turns brown as copper is obtained. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Hydrogen gas is passed over heated copper oxide. What happens?|id=ex-q-1>>
Let's write the reaction. Copper oxide plus hydrogen gives copper plus water. <<WRITE_STEP:CuO + H2 (heat) -> Cu + H2O|id=ex-step-1-1>>
Now look closely at what each substance does. The copper oxide loses oxygen, so the copper oxide is reduced. <<WRITE_STEP:Copper oxide loses oxygen -> reduced|id=ex-step-1-2>>

Meanwhile the hydrogen gains that oxygen to form water, so the hydrogen is oxidised. Reduction and oxidation happen together. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Copper oxide is reduced; hydrogen is oxidised - a redox reaction|id=ex-ans-1>>

Here's an example from the chapter. Consider this reaction: zinc oxide plus carbon gives zinc plus carbon monoxide. Let's figure out which substance is oxidised and which is reduced. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: In ZnO + C -> Zn + CO, identify what is oxidised and what is reduced|id=ex-q-1>>

First, look at the carbon. Carbon starts on its own and ends up combined with oxygen as carbon monoxide. Since carbon gains oxygen, carbon is oxidised to carbon monoxide. <<WRITE_STEP:Carbon gains oxygen, so carbon is oxidised to carbon monoxide|id=ex-step-1-1>>

Now look at the zinc oxide. It begins with oxygen attached and ends as plain zinc, having lost that oxygen. Since zinc oxide loses oxygen, zinc oxide is reduced to zinc. <<WRITE_STEP:Zinc oxide loses oxygen, so zinc oxide is reduced to zinc|id=ex-step-1-2>>
So in this reaction, carbon is oxidised to carbon monoxide, and zinc oxide is reduced to zinc. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Carbon is oxidised to carbon monoxide; zinc oxide is reduced to zinc|id=ex-ans-1>>

Here's an example from the chapter. Consider the reaction where manganese dioxide plus four hydrochloric acid gives manganese chloride plus two water plus chlorine. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Identify oxidation and reduction in MnO2 + 4HCl -> MnCl2 + 2H2O + Cl2|id=ex-q-1>>

Let's look at what happens to each species. The hydrochloric acid is oxidised to chlorine, because it loses electrons and gains oxygen character as it forms chlorine gas. <<WRITE_STEP:Hydrochloric acid is oxidised to chlorine|id=ex-step-1-1>> <<WRITE_EQUATION:MnO_2 + 4HCl \rightarrow MnCl_2 + 2H_2O + Cl_2|id=ex-eq-1>>

At the same time, the manganese dioxide is reduced to manganese chloride, because it loses oxygen and gains electrons. So we have both oxidation and reduction in the same reaction. <<WRITE_STEP:Manganese dioxide is reduced to manganese chloride|id=ex-step-1-2>> <<WRITE_ANSWER:Hydrochloric acid is oxidised to chlorine; manganese dioxide is reduced to manganese chloride|id=ex-ans-1>>
Because both happen together, we give the whole thing one name. We call it a redox reaction, short for reduction and oxidation.

<<WRITE_TEXT:Oxygen handed off: one gains, one loses|id=text-1>>So remember the picture: oxygen gets handed from one substance to another. Whoever takes it is oxidised, whoever gives it up is reduced, and the swap is redox.

equations.explanation_in_words: Two units of copper combine with one molecule of oxygen gas to give two units of black copper oxide.
Copper oxide plus hydrogen gives copper plus water, as the oxygen moves from the copper to the hydrogen.

lesson_plans.title: Corrosion: Why Metals Get Eaten Alive

hook.text: Leave a shiny new iron nail outside for a few weeks, and it comes back covered in flaky reddish-brown powder. Something has been quietly eating it.

crucial_facts: Corrosion is a metal being slowly attacked and eaten away by substances around it like moisture and air.
Rust on iron, the green coating on copper, and the black coating on silver are all corrosion.

diagrams.purpose: Show that rust on iron, green on copper, and black on silver are the same process happening to different metals, by placing the before-and-after of all three side by side.

required_elements.description: A bright shiny silvery iron nail labelled 'new iron'.
The same iron nail now coated in flaky reddish-brown rust.
A shiny orange-brown copper object, such as a small statue or coin.
The same copper object now coated with a dull green layer.
A bright reflective silver spoon.
The same silver spoon now coated with a dull black tarnish.
Arrows labelled 'moisture + air' pointing at all three metals to show what attacks them.

choreography.narration: Leave a shiny new iron nail outside for a few weeks, and it comes back covered in a flaky, reddish-brown powder. Something has been quietly eating it.
Here's the same nail before and after. The shine is gone, and in its place is rust. We call this the rusting of iron.
But here's a question worth pausing on: is iron the only metal this happens to, or is something bigger going on?
Look at copper. A bright orange statue left outside slowly grows a dull green coating. You've seen this on old domes and rooftops.
And silver. A gleaming spoon left in a drawer slowly turns black. That's not dirt you can wipe off, it's the silver itself changing.
So no, iron isn't special. Rust, green copper, and black silver are all the same story: a metal being attacked by the stuff around it.

<<SECTION:What corrosion is|id=sec-1>>What's doing the attacking? Mostly moisture and the air, sometimes acids. <<WRITE_TEXT:metal + moisture, air, acids|id=text-1>>When a metal is slowly eaten away like this, we say it corrodes.

<<WRITE_KEY:Corrosion = a metal being slowly attacked and eaten by its surroundings|id=key-1>>That process has a name: corrosion. Corrosion is a metal being slowly attacked and eaten away by the substances around it.
And remember oxidation from last time? Corrosion is exactly that, happening to a metal: the metal loses electrons to oxygen and is oxidised, which is why the surface changes colour.
This isn't just a curiosity. Corrosion eats car bodies, bridges, ships, and railings, and rusting iron especially costs an enormous amount of money to replace every single year.
So when you next spot rust on a gate, green on a statue, or black on a spoon, you're seeing one idea in three costumes: a metal quietly being attacked by the world around it.

lesson_plans.title: Rancidity: Why Old Chips Smell Off

hook.text: Open a packet of chips that's been sitting in the cupboard for months, and it hits you — that stale, almost paint-like smell. What actually happened to those chips?

crucial_facts: Rancidity is the oxidation of fats and oils by oxygen in the air, which spoils their smell and taste.
We slow rancidity by keeping oxygen away — air-tight containers, antioxidants, and flushing packets with nitrogen.

choreography.narration: Open a packet of chips that's been sitting in the cupboard for months, and it hits you — that stale, almost paint-like smell. What actually happened to those chips?
The chips didn't rot the way fruit goes mouldy. Something quieter happened — the oxygen in the air slowly attacked the oil they were fried in.

<<SECTION:Rancidity|id=sec-1>>Fats and oils react with oxygen from the air in a chemical reaction. And you already know its name — this is oxidation, the same kind of reaction where a substance gains oxygen.

<<WRITE_KEY:Rancidity = oxidation of fats and oils by air|id=key-1>>When fats and oils are oxidised, we say they go rancid — their smell and taste change for the worse. That single word, rancidity, is the whole story.
Here's the honest question, though: if it's just oxygen doing this, why doesn't every packet of chips on the shelf taste terrible the day you buy it?
Because oxidation is slow, and manufacturers fight it. The trick is simple — if oxygen causes rancidity, then take the oxygen away.
<<WRITE_STEP:Air-tight containers limit oxygen contact|id=step-1>>That's why oily food is sealed in air-tight containers — less air touching the fat means slower oxidation.

<<WRITE_STEP:Antioxidants are added to react with oxygen first|id=step-2>>It's also why packets list antioxidants. These are substances that get oxidised instead of the fat, taking the hit so the oil stays fresh.

<<WRITE_STEP:Chip bags flushed with nitrogen, not air|id=step-3>>And the cleverest trick — chip manufacturers flush the bag with nitrogen gas. Nitrogen is unreactive, so with no oxygen inside, the chips simply can't go rancid.
Squeeze a sealed chip packet and feel how puffy it is. That cushion isn't air — it's nitrogen, quietly protecting your snack.
<<WRITE_KEY:No oxygen, no rancidity|id=key-2>>So next time food smells off, you'll know the culprit: oxygen oxidising the fats and oils. Keep the oxygen out, and you keep the food fresh.

segments.raw_narration: If you weigh a sealed jar before and after a reaction fizzes away inside it, the scale does not move even a hair. So where does the new stuff come from?

segments.raw_narration: The answer is that nothing new is ever made. The atoms you start with are the exact same atoms you finish with, just rearranged into new partners.

segments.raw_narration: <<SECTION:Conservation of mass|id=sec-1>>This is the law of conservation of mass you met last year. Mass can neither be created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:product-side>> <<SECTION:Conservation of mass|id=sec-1>>This is the law of conservation of mass you met last year. Mass can neither be created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction.

segments.raw_narration: <<WRITE_KEY:Atoms in equals atoms out, for every element|id=key-1>>Said in plain terms, the number of atoms of each element stays exactly the same before and after. Count them on the left, count them on the right, and the two counts must match.

segments.raw_narration: For every element, the number of atoms on the reactant side equals the number of atoms on the product side.

segments.raw_narration: Watch how we check this. On the reactant side I tally up each kind of atom one element at a time.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:reactant-tally>> Watch how we check this. On the reactant side I tally up each kind of atom one element at a time.

segments.raw_narration: Now the product side. If every element's tally on the right matches the left, the equation is already balanced.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:product-tally>> Now the product side. If every element's tally on the right matches the left, the equation is already balanced. <<TRACE:product-tally>>

segments.raw_narration: Here is a reaction where zinc meets sulphuric acid to give zinc sulphate and hydrogen, and the count already matches on both sides.

segments.raw_narration: But what happens when a count does not match? Say there are four oxygen atoms on one side but only one on the other. Can we just shrink the formula?
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:subscript-lock>> But what happens when a count does not match? Say there are four oxygen atoms on one side but only one on the other. Can we just shrink the formula? <<PAUSE:long>>

segments.raw_narration: No. The little subscript numbers inside a formula are locked. Changing water from H two O to H O would turn it into a completely different substance.
segments.text_with_markers: <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:subscript-lock>> No. The little subscript numbers inside a formula are locked. Changing water from H two O to H O would turn it into a completely different substance. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: Instead, we place a big number in front of the whole formula. That number multiplies every atom in the cluster at once, like buying two identical boxes instead of repacking one.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:coefficient-slot>> Instead, we place a big number in front of the whole formula. That number multiplies every atom in the cluster at once, like buying two identical boxes instead of repacking one.

segments.raw_narration: <<WRITE_STEP:Adjust front coefficients until both tallies match|id=step-1>>We keep adjusting those front numbers until the reactant tally and the product tally agree for every single element.

segments.raw_narration: <<WRITE_TEXT:Big numbers in front, never the small subscripts|id=text-1>>So the whole method is just bookkeeping for atoms. Change the big numbers in front, never the small subscripts inside.

segments.raw_narration: And when both tallies finally match, every atom is accounted for, the mass is conserved, and the scale on that sealed jar stays perfectly still.

segments.raw_narration: Burn a log down to a pile of ash, weigh it, and the ash is lighter than the log you started with. Yet chemistry insists not one atom was destroyed.

segments.raw_narration: So where did the missing mass go? Hold that question, because the answer rewrites what you think a reaction even is.

segments.raw_narration: <<SECTION:Atoms are stubborn|id=sec-1>>Here is the first stubborn rule. During an ordinary chemical reaction, an atom of oxygen stays an atom of oxygen. It never becomes carbon, never becomes anything else.

During an ordinary chemical reaction, an atom of oxygen stays an atom of oxygen. It never becomes carbon, never becomes anything else. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: And atoms never vanish into nothing, and they never appear from nowhere. Whatever you started with, you still have, every last one.
segments.text_with_markers: And atoms never vanish into nothing, and they never appear from nowhere. Whatever you started with, you still have, every last one. <<POINT:atom-count-tally>> <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: But if the atoms are all the same and all still here, then how on earth do we get a brand-new substance out the other side?
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:reactant-cluster>> But if the atoms are all the same and all still here, then how on earth do we get a brand-new substance out the other side? <<PAUSE:long>>

segments.raw_narration: Watch the lines holding these atoms together. Those lines are bonds, and as the reaction begins, the old bonds break apart.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:old-bond>> Watch the lines holding these atoms together. Those lines are bonds, and as the reaction begins, the old bonds break apart. <<TRACE:old-bond>> <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: <<WRITE_KEY:Reaction = break old bonds, make new bonds|id=key-1>>Now the very same atoms link up in a new pattern, and fresh bonds form. The atoms are old; the arrangement is new.

segments.raw_narration: And there is your new substance. Same building blocks, a different structure. That is the whole secret of a chemical reaction.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:product-cluster>> And there is your new substance. Same building blocks, a different structure. That is the whole secret of a chemical reaction.

segments.raw_narration: <<WRITE_TEXT:Same atoms, new arrangement|id=text-1>>Count them. Every kind of atom appears exactly as many times on the right as it did on the left. Nothing gained, nothing lost.

segments.raw_narration: So back to our log. The missing mass did not disappear; its atoms floated off invisibly as carbon dioxide and water vapour. Catch those gases and the weight is exactly the same.

segments.raw_narration: Drop a little white powder into water, touch the beaker, and your fingers feel heat — no flame, yet the glass is warm. Something just happened inside.

Higher means more eager to react. <<POINT:iron-rung>> <<POINT:iron-rung>> Because iron is above copper, iron can reach down and displace copper from its compound. <<TRACE:displacement-direction>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:copper-rung>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Lower metal can't displace higher|id=text-1>>But run it the other way: would a copper nail dropped into iron sulphate ever pull the iron out? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:reactivity-arrow>> No, nothing happens, because copper is below iron on the ladder. The reactivity series decides the winner, and a lower metal can never displace a higher one. <<PAUSE:short>> Here's an example from the chapter. We take three iron nails and clean them by rubbing with sandpaper. Then we take two test tubes, marked A and B, and in each we pour about ten milliliters of copper sulphate solution, which is a clear blue color. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Why does an iron nail in copper sulphate solution turn brownish while the blue colour fades?|id=ex-q-1>> Iron metal reacts with copper sulphate solution to give iron sulphate solution and solid copper. <<WRITE_EQUATION:Fe(s) + CuSO_4(aq) \rightarrow FeSO_4(aq) + Cu(s)|id=eq-1|boxed>> Now we tie two iron nails together with a thread and immerse them carefully in test tube B for about twenty minutes, while we keep one nail aside for comparison. After twenty minutes, when we take the nails out, the nails turn brownish and the blue color of the solution fades. <<WRITE_STEP:Two nails immersed in test tube B for 20 minutes; one nail kept aside.|id=ex-step-1>> <<WRITE_STEP:Result: nails become brownish, blue colour fades.|id=ex-step-2>> This happens because iron is more reactive than copper, so iron displaces copper from the copper sulphate solution. The reaction is iron plus copper sulphate gives iron sulphate plus copper. The brown coating is the copper deposited on the nail, and the blue fades because the copper sulphate is used up. So the answer is that a displacement reaction takes place. <<WRITE_EQUATION:Fe(s) + CuSO_4(aq) \rightarrow FeSO_4(aq) + Cu(s)|id=ex-eq-1>> <<WRITE_ANSWER:Iron displaces copper: Fe + CuSO4 → FeSO4 + Cu — a displacement reaction.|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. We look at two more displacement reactions. In the first, zinc reacts with copper sulphate. In the second, lead reacts with copper chloride. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Zn + CuSO4 and Pb + CuCl2 — what gets displaced?|id=ex-q-1>> Let's work them out. Zinc plus copper sulphate gives zinc sulphate plus copper. <<WRITE_STEP:Zn(s) + CuSO4(aq) -> ZnSO4(aq) + Cu(s)|id=ex-step-1-1>> And lead plus copper chloride gives lead chloride plus copper. <<WRITE_STEP:Pb(s) + CuCl2(aq) -> PbCl2(aq) + Cu(s)|id=ex-step-1-2>> Why does this happen? Because zinc and lead are more reactive than copper, so each of them pushes copper out of its compound. The answer is that copper is displaced in both reactions. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Zn and Pb, being more reactive than Cu, displace copper from its compounds.|id=ex-ans-1>> Now we can write what actually happened in symbols: iron plus copper sulphate gives iron sulphate plus copper. <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> <<WRITE_KEY:Reactivity series decides who displaces whom|id=key-2>>So remember the whole idea in one line: the higher metal in the reactivity series displaces the lower one out of its compound, and never the reverse. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: Two perfectly clear liquids. You pour one into the other, and suddenly the mixture turns milky white with a solid settling at the bottom. Nobody added a powder, so where did that solid come from?
segments.text_with_markers: Two perfectly clear liquids. You pour one into the other, and suddenly the mixture turns milky white with a solid settling at the bottom. Nobody added a powder, so where did that solid come from? <<PAUSE:long>>

segments.raw_narration: Think of it like a dance. Each clear liquid holds a compound made of two parts: a positive partner and a negative partner, drifting around dissolved in the water.

segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:barium-ion>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Each compound = positive part + negative part|id=text-1>>In our case one liquid carries sodium holding hands with sulphate, and the other carries barium holding hands with chloride. <<POINT:barium-ion>>

segments.raw_narration: Now mix them, and the music starts. The partners swap: the positive part of one compound goes looking for the negative part of the other.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:swap-arrows>> Now mix them, and the music starts. The partners swap: the positive part of one compound goes looking for the negative part of the other. <<TRACE:swap-arrows>> <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: But here is the twist. When barium meets sulphate, the new pair they make refuses to stay dissolved in water.

segments.raw_narration: So that brand new barium sulphate pair clumps together and sinks. That cloudy white solid you saw was created right there in the swap, born from two clear liquids.
segments.text_with_markers: <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:precipitate-solid>> So that brand new barium sulphate pair clumps together and sinks. That cloudy white solid you saw was created right there in the swap, born from two clear liquids.

segments.raw_narration: Shiny copper, heated in a china dish, slowly turns jet black. Something from the air has crept into the metal.

segments.raw_narration: That something is oxygen. The air is full of it, and when copper gets hot, the oxygen molecules grab on.
segments.text_with_markers: That something is oxygen. The air is full of it, and when copper gets hot, the oxygen molecules grab on. <<POINT:oxygen-molecule>>

segments.raw_narration: <<SECTION:Gaining oxygen|id=sec-1>>Watch the oxygen move onto the copper. The shiny metal becomes black copper oxide.

segments.raw_narration: So here is a fair question. If gaining oxygen is oxidation, can we ever run this backwards and pull the oxygen back out?

topics.our_understanding:
Let's start with something you might have actually seen in your classroom: a thin strip of magnesium ribbon being burned. When you light it, it burns with a dazzling, almost blinding white flame, and when it's done, you're left with a soft white powder. That white powder is magnesium oxide. It forms because the magnesium reacts with the oxygen in the air. So a chemical reaction has happened, and we want a good way to describe it.

Now, you could describe this in a full sentence: when a magnesium ribbon is burnt in oxygen, it gets converted to magnesium oxide. That's perfectly correct, but it's long and clumsy. Imagine writing a whole paragraph every time you wanted to talk about a reaction. So chemists came up with a shorter way to say the same thing, and the simplest version of that is called a word-equation.

For our magnesium reaction, the word-equation reads: magnesium plus oxygen gives magnesium oxide. Notice how compact that is compared to the full sentence. Let's break down the parts. The substances you start with, the ones that get used up and changed during the reaction, are called the reactants. Here, those are magnesium and oxygen. The brand-new substance that gets created is called the product. Here, that's magnesium oxide.

There's a neat structure to how we write this. The reactants always go on the left-hand side, and if there's more than one, we connect them with a plus sign. The products always go on the right-hand side, again joined with a plus sign if there's more than one. Between the reactants and the products, we draw an arrow. That arrow isn't just decoration. The arrowhead points toward the products, and it tells you the direction the reaction is going, from what you started with to what you ended up with.

Why does this matter? Because as you study chemistry, you'll deal with hundreds of reactions, and a clear shorthand lets you see at a glance what's reacting and what's forming. The word-equation is your first step. Later you'll learn to make these even more precise using chemical symbols and formulas, but the idea stays exactly the same: reactants on the left, an arrow showing direction, and products on the right.

topics.orig_book_content:
1.1.1 Writing a Chemical Equation
Is there any other shorter way for representing chemical equations?
Chemical equations can be made more concise and useful if we use
chemical formulae instead of words. A chemical equation represents a
chemical reaction. If you recall formulae of magnesium, oxygen and
magnesium oxide, the above word-equation can be written as –
Mg + O2  →  MgO
(1.2)
Count and compare the number of atoms of each element on the
LHS and RHS of the arrow. Is the number of atoms of each element the
same on both the sides? If yes, then the equation is balanced. If not,
then the equation is unbalanced because the mass is not the same on
both sides of the equation. Such a chemical equation is a skeletal
chemical equation for a reaction. Equation (1.2) is a skeletal chemical
equation for the burning of magnesium in air.
topics.our_understanding:
Let's think about how chemists write down what happens in a reaction. You could describe a reaction using words, but that gets long and clumsy. So chemists found a shorter, smarter way: instead of writing out the names of substances, they use chemical formulae. That's really what a chemical equation is — a quick, symbolic way to represent a chemical reaction.

Take the burning of magnesium in air. In words, you'd say magnesium reacts with oxygen to give magnesium oxide. But if you remember the formulae — magnesium is just Mg, oxygen in the air travels as a pair of atoms so it's written as O two, and magnesium oxide is M g O — then you can write the whole thing compactly. On the left side you put magnesium plus oxygen, then an arrow pointing right, and on the right side you put magnesium oxide. The arrow means 'gives' or 'produces'. The stuff on the left of the arrow are the reactants, the things you start with. The stuff on the right are the products, what you end up with.

Now here's the important part. Once you've written this, you should count the atoms of each element on the left-hand side and compare them with the right-hand side. Ask yourself: is the number of atoms of each element the same on both sides? If the answer is yes, the equation is balanced. If the answer is no, the equation is unbalanced.

Why does this matter so much? Because of mass. In a chemical reaction, matter is not created or destroyed — the atoms just rearrange. So the total mass before and after must be the same. If your equation has different numbers of atoms on each side, that's like claiming mass appeared or vanished, which can't happen. That's why an unbalanced equation is described as having unequal mass on both sides.

When you first write the equation just from formulae, without yet fixing the atom counts, we call it a skeletal chemical equation. It's like a rough draft — the bones of the reaction are there, but it isn't necessarily balanced yet. So the magnesium-burning equation we just wrote is a skeletal equation. In the next step, we'll learn how to balance it so that every element matches up on both sides.

topics.orig_book_content:
1.1.2 Balanced Chemical Equations
Recall the law of conservation of mass that you studied in Class IX; mass
can neither be created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction. That is, the

topics.our_understanding:
Let's talk about why we balance chemical equations. Remember the law of conservation of mass from last year? It says that mass can never be created or destroyed in a chemical reaction. So whatever atoms you start with, you must end with. The total mass of the elements in the products has to equal the total mass of the elements in the reactants. Said another way, the number of atoms of each element stays exactly the same before and after the reaction. That's the whole reason balancing matters — atoms don't vanish and they don't appear out of nowhere.

Let's see this in action. When zinc reacts with sulphuric acid, we get zinc sulphate and hydrogen. If you count the atoms on each side, you find one zinc on the left and one on the right, two hydrogens on each side, one sulphur on each side, and four oxygens on each side. Everything matches, so that equation is already balanced.

But many equations don't start out balanced. Take iron reacting with water to give iron oxide and hydrogen. Here's the step-by-step trick. First, draw boxes around each formula, and promise yourself you won't change anything inside those boxes — that means you can put a number in front of a formula, but you can never change the formula itself. Next, count atoms of each element on both sides. You'll notice they don't match. A smart move is to start with the compound that has the most atoms — in our case that's the iron oxide — and balance the element appearing most, which is oxygen. There are four oxygens on the right and one on the left, so we put a four in front of water. Then we fix hydrogen, then iron, adjusting one element at a time, always using the smallest whole numbers. When every element finally matches, we're done. This trial-by-trial approach is fittingly called the hit-and-trial method.

There's one more polish. We can make an equation more informative by adding the physical state of each substance. We write little symbols: g for gas, l for liquid, aq for aqueous, meaning dissolved in water, and s for solid. Sometimes we also note conditions like temperature, pressure, or a catalyst above or below the arrow. These extras tell us not just what reacts, but how and in what form.

We have learnt in Class IX that during a chemical reaction atoms of one
element do not change into those of another element. Nor do atoms
disappear from the mixture or appear from elsewhere. Actually, chemical
reactions involve the breaking and making of bonds between atoms to
produce new substances. You will study about types of bonds formed
between atoms in Chapters 3 and 4.
topics.our_understanding: Let's set the stage for what's coming in this part of the chapter. You already learned something important back in Class nine, and it's worth pausing to really feel why it matters. During a chemical reaction, the atoms themselves don't transform into different kinds of atoms. An atom of, say, oxygen stays an atom of oxygen. It doesn't suddenly become an atom of carbon or anything else. That's a fixed rule in ordinary chemistry. So if atoms can't change their identity, what's actually happening when a reaction takes place? And just as importantly, atoms don't vanish into nothing, and they don't magically appear out of nowhere. Whatever atoms you started with, you still have them all by the end. They're just arranged differently. Think about this like rearranging a set of building blocks. You don't get new blocks, and you don't lose any. You simply take them apart and put them back together in a new pattern. That's exactly what a chemical reaction is doing at the tiniest level. The atoms in the starting substances are held together by connections we call bonds. During a reaction, some of those bonds break apart, and then new bonds form between the atoms in fresh combinations. Because the atoms get linked up in new ways, you end up with new substances that have different properties from what you began with. This is the heart of why reactions produce something genuinely new, even though no atom was created or destroyed. Notice how this single idea quietly explains a lot. It tells you why mass is conserved, since every atom is accounted for. It tells you why we can write balanced equations, because the count of each kind of atom has to match on both sides. And it hints at a deeper question we haven't answered yet: what exactly are these bonds, and why do atoms form them in the first place? That's a story for later chapters, where you'll study the different types of bonds that hold atoms together. For now, hold onto this key picture: chemical reactions are all about breaking old bonds and making new ones, rearranging the same atoms into new substances. Keep that image in your mind as we go on to explore the different families, or types, of chemical reactions.

topics.our_understanding:
Let's talk about one of the simplest and most satisfying kinds of chemical change: the combination reaction. The idea is right there in the name. When two or more substances come together and join up to make a single new product, we call that a combination reaction. Two things go in, one thing comes out. That's the heart of it.

Think about the classic example with quick lime, which is calcium oxide. Imagine you take a little of this white powder in a beaker and slowly add water to it. If you touch the beaker, you'll feel it getting warm, sometimes quite hot. What's happening is that calcium oxide and water are combining to form a single new product called calcium hydroxide, which we also call slaked lime. Notice that two reactants, the calcium oxide and the water, came together to give just one product. That's exactly what makes it a combination reaction.

Now here's a second important idea hiding in this same experiment. That warmth you felt? It tells you the reaction is releasing heat. Any reaction in which heat is given out along with the products is called an exothermic reaction. So this calcium oxide and water reaction is both a combination reaction and an exothermic one. The two categories can overlap.

There are other combination reactions worth knowing. When coal burns, the carbon in it combines with oxygen from the air to form carbon dioxide. When hydrogen gas reacts with oxygen gas, they combine to form water. In each case, simpler substances join up into a single product.

Exothermic reactions are everywhere, even inside you. When natural gas burns, it releases heat. And here's something surprising: the very act of breathing involves an exothermic reaction. The food you eat, like rice, potatoes, and bread, gets broken down into glucose. That glucose then combines with oxygen inside your body's cells to release the energy that keeps you alive. We call this process respiration. Even rotting vegetable matter turning into compost gives off heat, so that's exothermic too.

One last lovely real-world connection: the slaked lime made from that calcium oxide reaction is used to whitewash walls. Over two to three days, the calcium hydroxide reacts slowly with carbon dioxide in the air to form a thin shiny layer of calcium carbonate, giving walls that clean finish. And interestingly, calcium carbonate is the very same compound that makes up marble. So a simple combination reaction connects your beaker to the walls of your home and to marble statues.

topics.our_understanding:
Let's talk about decomposition reactions. The name gives away the idea: in a decomposition reaction, a single substance breaks down, or splits apart, into two or more simpler substances. Think of it as the opposite of building something — instead of joining pieces together, we're taking one thing and pulling it into parts. To make this happen, we usually have to supply energy, and that energy can come in different forms: heat, light, or electricity.

When we use heat to break a compound apart, we call it thermal decomposition. For example, when you heat lead nitrate, it breaks down into lead oxide, nitrogen dioxide gas, and oxygen gas. So one solid compound turns into a solid plus two gases — all because we added heat.

Now let's bring in light. Imagine you have about two grams of silver chloride in a china dish. It starts out white. But if you leave it sitting in sunlight for a while, you'll notice it slowly turns grey. What's happening? The sunlight is supplying energy that breaks the silver chloride apart into silver metal — that's the grey colour you see — and chlorine gas, which escapes. So light alone can drive a decomposition. This particular reaction is actually used in black-and-white photography.

Third, we can use electricity to decompose a substance, and this is called electrolysis. Picture a plastic mug filled with water, with two carbon electrodes connected to a six volt battery, and a few drops of dilute sulphuric acid added to help the water conduct. When you switch on the current, bubbles form at both electrodes. These are the two gases that water is made of — hydrogen and oxygen. Here's something neat to notice: the gas collected at one electrode is exactly double the amount collected at the other. That's because water contains twice as many hydrogen atoms as oxygen atoms, so you get twice as much hydrogen gas. You can test which gas is which by bringing a burning candle close — hydrogen burns with a pop, while oxygen makes the flame burn more brightly.

So the big takeaway is this: decomposition reactions take one substance and split it into simpler ones, and we always need to add energy — heat, light, or electricity — to make the breakdown happen. Whenever you see something falling apart into pieces with energy added, you're looking at a decomposition reaction.

topics.our_understanding: Let's talk about displacement reactions, and the best way in is through a simple experiment you can almost picture in your hands. Imagine you take three iron nails and rub them clean with sandpaper until they shine. Then you fill two test tubes with about ten milliliters of copper sulphate solution each. Copper sulphate solution has a lovely blue color, so remember that. You tie two of your nails together with a thread and lower them into one test tube, leaving the other test tube alone for comparison, and you keep one nail aside, untouched, so you can compare it later. Now you wait about twenty minutes and watch what happens. When you pull the nails out, two changes jump out at you. First, the iron nails have turned a brownish color, like they got coated with something. Second, the blue color of the solution they were sitting in has faded compared to the test tube you left alone. So what's going on here? The iron has kicked the copper out of the copper sulphate. We say iron displaces copper. The brown coating on the nail is actual copper metal that came out of solution and stuck to the iron. And the blue fades because the copper sulphate, which gave the blue color, is being turned into iron sulphate, which is much paler. So in words, iron plus copper sulphate gives iron sulphate plus copper. That's the heart of it. This is called a displacement reaction, because one element pushes another element out of its compound and takes its place. Now here's the key idea that makes all of this make sense. A more reactive element can displace a less reactive one. Iron is more reactive than copper, so iron can shove copper aside. The same thing happens with zinc and lead. Zinc plus copper sulphate gives zinc sulphate plus copper, and lead plus copper chloride gives lead chloride plus copper. Both zinc and lead are more reactive than copper, so they too displace copper from its compounds. Think of it like a more popular kid taking the front seat. The more reactive element wins the spot in the compound, and the less reactive one gets pushed out as a free metal. Once you understand this reactivity idea, you can start predicting which displacement reactions will actually happen and which won't.

topics.our_understanding:
Let's explore a special kind of chemical reaction called a double displacement reaction. The word displacement means swapping, and double means it happens twice. So imagine two compounds dissolved in water, each made of two parts. In a double displacement reaction, these two compounds trade partners. The positive part of one pairs up with the negative part of the other, and the leftover pieces pair up too. It's like a partner swap at a dance.

Here's the activity the book walks us through. Take about three milliliters of sodium sulphate solution in a test tube. In another test tube, take about three milliliters of barium chloride solution. Now mix the two solutions together. What do you observe? You'll see a white substance form, one that does not dissolve in water. This insoluble solid is called a precipitate. Think of it as a solid that suddenly appears out of two clear liquids and settles down because it can't stay dissolved.

Because a precipitate forms, we give this reaction a second name too. Any reaction that produces a precipitate can be called a precipitation reaction. So the same reaction can be described two ways depending on what we want to highlight.

Now let's see the swap. Sodium sulphate in solution reacts with barium chloride in solution. The sodium and the barium switch partners. The barium joins with the sulphate to form barium sulphate, which is the solid white precipitate. Meanwhile the sodium joins with the chloride to form sodium chloride, which stays dissolved in the water. Notice how each compound handed off one of its parts to the other. That double exchange is exactly why we call it double displacement.

The key insight to carry away is this: in a double displacement reaction, ions in two compounds exchange to give two new compounds. Often one of those new compounds is insoluble, and that's the precipitate you can actually see forming with your eyes. Watching a white solid appear when you pour two clear liquids together is one of the most satisfying signs that a real chemical change has just taken place. That visible change is your clue that the atoms have rearranged into brand new substances.

topics.our_understanding:
Let's talk about two words that go hand in hand in chemistry: oxidation and reduction. Imagine you take about one gram of copper powder and heat it in a china dish. As it heats, the shiny copper surface turns into a black coating. That black stuff is copper oxide. Why did it form? Because oxygen from the air joined with the copper. When copper combines with oxygen, two units of copper plus one molecule of oxygen gas give you two units of copper oxide. Whenever a substance gains oxygen during a reaction, we say it has been oxidised.

Now here's the neat reverse. If you take that black copper oxide and pass hydrogen gas over it while it's hot, the black coating turns brown again, and you get copper back. In this reaction, copper oxide plus hydrogen gives copper plus water. Notice what happened: the copper oxide lost its oxygen, so we say it was reduced. The hydrogen grabbed that oxygen, so the hydrogen was oxidised. When a substance loses oxygen during a reaction, it is said to be reduced.

Here's the key insight that ties it all together. In a single reaction, one reactant gets oxidised at the very same time another gets reduced. You can't have one without the other. These paired reactions are called oxidation-reduction reactions, or redox reactions for short. Think of it like a handoff: oxygen leaves one partner and lands on another.

Let's look at a couple more examples. When zinc oxide reacts with carbon, the carbon gains oxygen to become carbon monoxide, so carbon is oxidised, while the zinc oxide loses its oxygen to become plain zinc, so it is reduced. In another reaction, manganese dioxide reacts with hydrochloric acid to give manganese chloride, water, and chlorine gas. Here the hydrochloric acid is oxidised to chlorine, while the manganese dioxide is reduced to manganese chloride.

Finally, we can stretch the definition a bit wider. Oxidation isn't only about gaining oxygen, and reduction isn't only about losing it. If a substance gains oxygen or loses hydrogen, it is oxidised. If a substance loses oxygen or gains hydrogen, it is reduced. Keep that broader picture in mind, because in everyday life these redox reactions show up all the time, like rusting iron or food going bad.
