1.3.1 Corrosion
You must have observed that iron articles are shiny when new, but get
coated with a reddish brown powder when left for some time. This process
is commonly known as rusting of iron. Some other metals also get
tarnished in this manner. Have you noticed the colour of the coating
formed on copper and silver? When a metal is attacked by substances
around it such as moisture, acids, etc., it is said to corrode and this
process is called corrosion. The black coating on silver and the green
coating on copper are other examples of corrosion.
Corrosion causes damage to car bodies, bridges, iron railings, ships
and to all objects made of metals, specially those of iron. Corrosion of
iron is a serious problem. Every year an enormous amount of money is
spent to replace damaged iron. You will learn more about corrosion in
Chapter 3.
topics.our_understanding:
Let me ask you something you've probably noticed without thinking too hard about it. When you buy a brand new iron object, like a nail or a gate, it looks shiny and bright. But leave that same iron outside for a few weeks or months, and what happens? It gets covered with a flaky, reddish brown powder. We call this rusting of iron, and it's something you can see all around you on old railings, bicycles, and tools.

Now here's the bigger idea. Iron isn't the only metal that changes over time. Think about copper and silver too. Have you ever seen an old copper object, like a statue or a pot? It develops a greenish coating. And silver, like jewelry or spoons left out, slowly turns black. These color changes are all telling us the same story. The metal is being attacked by things in its surroundings, such as moisture in the air and acids. When a metal gets attacked like this, we say it corrodes, and the whole process is called corrosion.

So rusting is just one specific example of corrosion, the kind that happens to iron. The green on copper and the black on silver are other examples of corrosion happening to different metals. Notice that each metal gives a different color, but the underlying idea is the same. The metal reacts with stuff around it and forms a new substance on its surface.

Why should you care about this? Because corrosion is not just a small cosmetic problem. It causes real damage to things we depend on, like car bodies, bridges, iron railings, ships, and basically anything made of metal, especially iron. Think about how serious that is. A bridge weakened by rust, or a ship hull eaten away, can be dangerous. And it's expensive too. Every single year, an enormous amount of money is spent to replace iron that has been damaged by corrosion. So understanding corrosion isn't just curiosity, it actually saves money and keeps things safe. As you go further in chemistry, you'll learn more about why corrosion happens and how we can slow it down or prevent it. For now, the key thing to remember is that corrosion is a chemical change where metals react with their environment and slowly get spoiled.

topics.our_understanding:
Let's talk about something you've probably experienced at home without even realizing it had a scientific name. Have you ever opened a packet of chips or smelled some cooking oil that's been sitting around too long, and noticed that it smells off, sometimes even nasty? That change has a name, and it's called rancidity.

Here's what's happening. Fats and oils in our food can react with the oxygen in the air around them. This is a type of chemical reaction called oxidation. When fats and oils are oxidised, they go rancid, which means their smell and their taste change for the worse. So the food doesn't actually rot in the usual way, but the oxygen slowly attacks the fat and oil molecules and turns them into something that smells and tastes bad.

Now, the really useful part is what we can do about it, because once you understand the cause, you understand the cure. Since the problem is oxidation, anything that slows down or prevents oxidation will help keep the food fresh. So food makers add special substances called antioxidants. The word literally tells you what they do, they work against oxidation. By adding these to foods that contain fats and oils, they slow down the spoiling.

Another simple trick is to keep food in air tight containers. Think about why that works. If the air can't get in, then the oxygen can't reach the fat and oil, so the oxidation slows right down. Less oxygen means less rancidity.

And here's a clever real world example to remember. Chip manufacturers flush their bags of chips with a gas like nitrogen before sealing them. Why nitrogen? Because nitrogen doesn't react with the food the way oxygen does. By pushing out the oxygen and replacing it with nitrogen, they protect the chips from getting oxidised, so the chips stay crisp and fresh for much longer. That little puff of air you feel when you open a chip bag is mostly nitrogen doing its protective job.

So the big idea connecting all of this is oxidation. Rancidity is oxidation of fats and oils, and every method we use to prevent it works by keeping oxygen away or by adding chemicals that fight oxidation. Once you see that pattern, it all makes sense together.

events.text: Rancidity = oxidation of fats and oils by air
Air-tight containers limit oxygen contact
Antioxidants are added to react with oxygen first
Chip bags flushed with nitrogen, not air
No oxygen, no rancidity

topics.standalone_narration_text: Open a packet of chips that's been sitting in the cupboard for months, and it hits you — that stale, almost paint-like smell. What actually happened to those chips? The chips didn't rot the way fruit goes mouldy. Something quieter happened — the oxygen in the air slowly attacked the oil they were fried in. <<SECTION:Rancidity|id=sec-1>>Fats and oils react with oxygen from the air in a chemical reaction. And you already know its name — this is oxidation, the same kind of reaction where a substance gains oxygen. <<WRITE_KEY:Rancidity = oxidation of fats and oils by air|id=key-1>>When fats and oils are oxidised, we say they go rancid — their smell and taste change for the worse. That single word, rancidity, is the whole story. <<PAUSE:short>> Here's the honest question, though: if it's just oxygen doing this, why doesn't every packet of chips on the shelf taste terrible the day you buy it? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> Because oxidation is slow, and manufacturers fight it. The trick is simple — if oxygen causes rancidity, then take the oxygen away. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_STEP:Air-tight containers limit oxygen contact|id=step-1>>That's why oily food is sealed in air-tight containers — less air touching the fat means slower oxidation. <<WRITE_STEP:Antioxidants are added to react with oxygen first|id=step-2>>It's also why packets list antioxidants. These are substances that get oxidised instead of the fat, taking the hit so the oil stays fresh. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_STEP:Chip bags flushed with nitrogen, not air|id=step-3>>And the cleverest trick — chip manufacturers flush the bag with nitrogen gas. Nitrogen is unreactive, so with no oxygen inside, the chips simply can't go rancid. <<PAUSE:short>> Squeeze a sealed chip packet and feel how puffy it is. That cushion isn't air — it's nitrogen, quietly protecting your snack. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:No oxygen, no rancidity|id=key-2>>So next time food smells off, you'll know the culprit: oxygen oxidising the fats and oils. Keep the oxygen out, and you keep the food fresh. <<PAUSE:short>>

questions.q_text: When hydrogen reacts with oxygen, water is produced. Write the word-equation for this reaction, and identify the reactants and the product.
questions.answer: Step 1: Identify the substances you start with (reactants). These are hydrogen and oxygen, because they get used up and changed during the reaction. questions.q_text: The skeletal equation for burning magnesium is written as Mg plus O two gives MgO. Count the atoms of each element on both sides and state whether this equation is balanced or unbalanced.
questions.answer: First, list the elements: magnesium (Mg) and oxygen (O). On the left-hand side we have: magnesium — 1 atom (from Mg), and oxygen — 2 atoms (from O two, since oxygen travels as a pair of atoms). On the right-hand side we have: magnesium — 1 atom (from MgO), and oxygen — 1 atom (from MgO). Now compare: magnesium is 1 on the left and 1 on the right — equal. Oxygen is 2 on the left but only 1 on the right — not equal. Since the number of oxygen atoms differs between the two sides, the equation is unbalanced. This means the mass is not equal on both sides as written, so it is only a skeletal equation that still needs balancing.

questions.q_text: Balance the equation for iron reacting with water to give iron oxide (Fe3O4) and hydrogen gas. The unbalanced form is: Fe + H2O gives Fe3O4 + H2.
questions.answer: Start by listing atoms. On the left: 1 Fe, 2 H, 1 O. On the right: 3 Fe, 4 O, 2 H. Begin with the compound having the most atoms, which is Fe3O4, and balance the element appearing most, oxygen. There are 4 oxygens on the right and only 1 on the left, so put a 4 in front of water: Fe + 4 H2O gives Fe3O4 + H2. Now recount left: 1 Fe, 8 H, 4 O. Next balance hydrogen. The left now has 8 H, the right has 2 H, so put a 4 in front of H2 on the right: Fe + 4 H2O gives Fe3O4 + 4 H2. Now hydrogen is 8 on each side and oxygen is 4 on each side. Finally balance iron: the right has 3 Fe, the left has 1 Fe, so put a 3 in front of Fe: 3 Fe + 4 H2O gives Fe3O4 + 4 H2. Check: Fe = 3 each side, H = 8 each side, O = 4 each side. The balanced equation is 3 Fe + 4 H2O gives Fe3O4 + 4 H2.

questions.q_text: For the reaction of zinc with sulphuric acid giving zinc sulphate and hydrogen, written as Zn + H2SO4 gives ZnSO4 + H2, verify whether it is balanced by counting the atoms of each element.
questions.answer: Count each element on both sides. Zinc: 1 on the left (Zn), 1 on the right (in ZnSO4) — matches. Hydrogen: 2 on the left (in H2SO4), 2 on the right (in H2) — matches. Sulphur: 1 on the left (in H2SO4), 1 on the right (in ZnSO4) — matches. Oxygen: 4 on the left (in H2SO4), 4 on the right (in ZnSO4) — matches. Since the number of atoms of every element is equal on both sides, the equation is already balanced.

questions.q_text: The text compares a chemical reaction to rearranging building blocks. Explain how this analogy captures what happens to atoms and bonds during a reaction.
questions.answer: In the building-block analogy, the blocks represent atoms and the way they are joined represents the bonds. Step one: you start with a certain set of blocks (the atoms in the reactants), connected in a particular pattern. Step two: you take the structure apart — this represents breaking the existing bonds. Step three: you put the blocks back together in a new pattern — this represents forming new bonds in fresh combinations. Throughout the process you never get any new blocks and you never lose any; you have exactly the same set you started with. This matches a real reaction: atoms are not created or destroyed, only rearranged. Because the same atoms are now linked in new ways, the result is new substances with different properties — just as rearranging blocks gives you a new structure even though the pieces are unchanged. This also explains conservation of mass, since every block (atom) is still present at the end.

questions.q_text: Explain why a freshly whitewashed wall, painted with slaked lime, develops a hard shiny white finish after two to three days. Name the compound responsible and state its connection to marble.
questions.answer: Step 1: Whitewashing uses slaked lime, which is calcium hydroxide. Step 2: Over two to three days, this calcium hydroxide reacts slowly with carbon dioxide present in the air. Step 3: This reaction is a combination reaction, since the calcium hydroxide and carbon dioxide come together to form a single new product, calcium carbonate (water is also released, but the key new solid is calcium carbonate). Step 4: The thin layer of calcium carbonate that forms is hard and shiny, which gives the wall its clean white finish. Step 5: The connection to marble is that marble is made of the very same compound, calcium carbonate, so the shiny coating on the wall is chemically identical to the material of marble statues.

questions.q_text: When lead nitrate is heated strongly, it undergoes thermal decomposition. Identify the products formed and explain what type of reaction this is and why.
questions.answer: Step 1: Recognise the process. Lead nitrate is a single compound, and we are supplying heat. When one substance breaks into simpler substances on adding energy, it is a decomposition reaction. Because the energy is supplied as heat, it is specifically a thermal decomposition. Step 2: Identify the products. Heating lead nitrate breaks it down into lead oxide (a solid), nitrogen dioxide gas, and oxygen gas. Step 3: Summarise. So one solid compound turns into a solid plus two gases. This fits the definition of decomposition: a single starting substance splits into multiple simpler products, made possible by the heat energy added.

questions.q_text: In the electrolysis of water, you collect a gas at each of the two electrodes. Describe how you could test each gas to find out which one is hydrogen and which one is oxygen.
questions.answer: Step 1: Recall the two gases produced. Water decomposes into hydrogen and oxygen, with hydrogen collected in double the amount of oxygen. Step 2: Test the gas present in the larger amount. Bring a burning candle close to it. If it burns with a 'pop' sound, that gas is hydrogen. Step 3: Test the gas present in the smaller amount. Bring a burning candle (or glowing splint) close to it. If it makes the flame burn more brightly, that gas is oxygen, because oxygen supports combustion. Step 4: Conclusion. The 'pop' test identifies hydrogen, and the brighter, more vigorous flame identifies oxygen. The greater volume of gas is hydrogen, confirming that water is made of twice as much hydrogen as oxygen.

questions.q_text: Zinc is more reactive than copper. Write, in words, what happens when zinc is added to copper sulphate solution, and explain why this reaction occurs.
questions.answer: Step 1: Identify the reactants — we have zinc metal and copper sulphate solution. Step 2: Apply the reactivity rule — a more reactive element can displace a less reactive one. Since zinc is more reactive than copper, zinc will push the copper out of copper sulphate and take its place. Step 3: Write the word equation — zinc plus copper sulphate gives zinc sulphate plus copper. Step 4: Explain the observations — the copper that is displaced comes out as free copper metal, and the blue copper sulphate is converted into the paler zinc sulphate, so the blue color would fade. This is a displacement reaction because zinc, being more reactive, occupies the spot in the compound and copper gets pushed out as a free metal.

questions.q_text: When solutions of sodium sulphate and barium chloride are mixed, identify the two new compounds formed and explain which ions swap partners.
questions.answer: Sodium sulphate is made of sodium (positive part) and sulphate (negative part). Barium chloride is made of barium (positive part) and chloride (negative part). In the double displacement reaction, the positive parts swap their negative partners. Step 1: The barium pairs with the sulphate to form barium sulphate. Since barium sulphate is insoluble in water, it appears as the white solid precipitate. Step 2: The sodium pairs with the chloride to form sodium chloride, which remains dissolved in the water. So the two new compounds are barium sulphate (the precipitate) and sodium chloride (dissolved). Each original compound handed off one of its ions to the other, which is exactly why it is called a double displacement reaction.

B. Because oxygen leaves one substance and is gained by another at the same time
C. Because both substances always gain oxygen
D. Because they happen in separate reactions but are studied together

questions.q_text: When hot copper oxide is passed over hydrogen gas, copper and water are formed. Identify which substance is oxidised and which is reduced, and explain your reasoning.
questions.answer: Step 1: Write what happens in the reaction. Copper oxide plus hydrogen gives copper plus water. Step 2: Track the oxygen. The copper oxide started with oxygen attached to copper, but ended up as plain copper, so it lost its oxygen. Losing oxygen means it was reduced. Step 3: Track the hydrogen. The hydrogen gas started with no oxygen, but ended up combined with oxygen as water, so it gained oxygen. Gaining oxygen means it was oxidised. Step 4: Conclusion. Copper oxide is reduced (it lost oxygen) and hydrogen is oxidised (it gained oxygen). This is a redox reaction because both happen together.

questions.q_text: Manganese dioxide reacts with hydrochloric acid to give manganese chloride, water, and chlorine gas. Identify what is oxidised and what is reduced.
questions.answer: Step 1: Look at the manganese dioxide. It contains oxygen bound to manganese, but it ends up as manganese chloride, which no longer has that oxygen. So manganese dioxide lost oxygen, meaning it was reduced. Step 2: Look at the hydrochloric acid. It contains hydrogen and chlorine. In the products, chlorine gas is released, which means the hydrochloric acid lost hydrogen. Losing hydrogen counts as being oxidised under the broader definition. So the hydrochloric acid is oxidised to chlorine. Step 3: Conclusion. Manganese dioxide is reduced and hydrochloric acid is oxidised, making this a redox reaction.

questions.q_text: When zinc oxide reacts with carbon, the carbon becomes carbon monoxide and the zinc oxide becomes zinc. Which statement is correct?
options: A. Carbon is reduced and zinc oxide is oxidised
B. Carbon is oxidised and zinc oxide is reduced
C. Both carbon and zinc oxide are oxidised
D. Both carbon and zinc oxide are reduced

questions.q_text: An old copper statue develops a coating over time. What color is this coating, and what does it indicate?

questions.q_text: Why is corrosion considered more than just a cosmetic problem?

questions.q_text: A student leaves a shiny new iron nail outside for several weeks and finds it covered in a flaky reddish brown powder. Explain what has happened to the nail and why, using the idea of corrosion.
questions.answer: Step 1: Recognize the observation. The shiny iron nail has become coated with a flaky, reddish brown powder. This is rust. Step 2: Identify the process. Rusting is a specific example of corrosion, the kind that happens to iron. Step 3: Explain the cause. The iron has been attacked by things in its surroundings, mainly moisture in the air and acids. Step 4: Explain the result. The iron reacted with these substances in its environment and formed a new substance (rust) on its surface, which appears as the reddish brown flaky powder. Step 5: Conclusion. This is a chemical change, because a new substance with different properties has formed. The nail has corroded, meaning it has slowly been spoiled by reacting with its environment.

questions.q_text: Which of the following best describes what happens when food becomes rancid?

questions.q_text: Why do chip manufacturers flush their bags with nitrogen gas before sealing them?

questions.q_text: Keeping fatty foods in airtight containers slows down rancidity. What is the main reason this works?

questions.q_text: Based on what their name tells you, what do antioxidants do when added to food?

questions.q_text: A shopkeeper stores cooking oil in a clear glass bottle left open near a sunny window. The oil keeps going rancid quickly. Suggest two changes the shopkeeper could make to keep the oil fresh longer, and explain why each change helps.
questions.answer: Step 1: Identify the cause. Rancidity is the oxidation of fats and oils, meaning the oil reacts with oxygen in the air and develops a bad smell and taste. So anything that keeps oxygen away or fights oxidation will help. Step 2: First change — keep the oil in an airtight, sealed container instead of an open bottle. This stops air, and therefore oxygen, from reaching the oil, so oxidation slows right down and the oil stays fresh longer. Step 3: Second change — the manufacturer or shopkeeper could ensure the oil contains antioxidants, substances that work against oxidation and slow the spoiling. (Storing it away from sunlight and heat also helps, since these can speed up oxidation.) Conclusion: Both fixes work on the same principle — reducing oxidation by limiting oxygen contact or by adding chemicals that fight oxidation.
